The library therefore offers no eviction charge for Michigan; recover your costs through the court's judgment. Accelerated rent is never rent due for a nonpayment demand, and a separate claim for damages for breach may be joined in the eviction case.

title: Penalty for Knowingly Using a Prohibited Term
bodyText: Michigan penalizes knowingly using a prohibited lease term. Ordinarily a tenant who objects to a term barred by the Truth in Renting Act must first give you written notice and 20 days to cure it by written notice to every current tenant. That step is skipped, and the tenant may sue at once, if you actually knew the term was unlawful when the lease was signed, or a court of record already held the same term unlawful in a case you were a party to. Actual knowledge is shown only by a writing from you or an agent authorized to sign leases, an admission by you or such an agent, or your own earlier cure notice about the same term. The tenant may sue to void the lease and end the tenancy, for an order barring the term and requiring cure notices to all your tenants, and for $250 per action (or $500 where the term is explicitly and unambiguously prohibited or a required statement is missing), or actual damages if greater; the winner recovers court costs plus statutory attorney fees. A commercial seller of a printed lease form containing such a term is liable to a landlord who bought it. A term that also violates the Consumer Protection Act, such as an unclear waiver of a legal right, can carry that act's remedy too: actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees. Saying elsewhere in the lease that nothing limits the tenant's rights does not make a void term safe; leave such terms out.

title: No Waiver of the Notice to Quit in Michigan
bodyText: The default notices in Michigan: a tenancy at will or by sufferance, including month-to-month, ends on 1 month's notice, or notice equal to the rent interval where rent is paid more often than every 3 months; a year-to-year tenancy ends only by a notice to quit taking effect 1 year after service; a tenant who does not pay rent may be given a written 7-day notice to quit, or served a written 7-day demand for possession; and shorter notices apply where the lease has a clause allowing termination for drug activity on the premises and a formal police report has been filed (24 hours), and after the tenant, a household member or a person under the tenant's control caused or threatened physical injury to someone on property you own or operate and the police were notified (7 days), unless the person injured or threatened is the tenant or a household member or applying the rule would violate federal housing regulations. A fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term without notice. No Michigan statute lets a lease shorten or waive these notices. A lease term that waives or alters any right of notice or procedure required by law in a court case under the lease, or a party's rights in eviction (summary) proceedings, is void, and including it exposes you to the Truth in Renting Act's remedies. Whether a notice to quit given before suit counts as such a right is not settled by statute, so the library treats every statutory notice and demand as one that a lease cannot shorten or waive, and offers no waiver clause for Michigan.

title: No Confession of Judgment in a Michigan Lease
bodyText: A Michigan lease may not provide for a confession of judgment by either party; such a term is void and exposes you to the Truth in Renting Act's remedies. Outside a lease, Michigan allows a judgment by confession only in circuit court, on a plea signed by an attorney, and only if the authority to confess is in a separate instrument distinct from the contract for the debt and is produced and filed when the judgment is entered. No Michigan statute or court rule provides confessed judgment for possession of a home; an eviction goes through summary proceedings in district court. The library offers no confession of judgment and no separate authority to confess for Michigan.

title: Exemption Waivers Not Offered in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan's Constitution exempts a homestead and a resident's personal property, in amounts set by law, from forced sale on execution, and Michigan statutes exempt, among other things, family pictures, clothing and 6 months' provisions and fuel, household goods, furniture, utensils, books and appliances up to $1,000, and a homestead up to $3,500. The homestead exemption protects a dwelling the debtor owns and occupies, including a house the debtor owns on land the debtor does not own (such as a mobile home on a rented lot); a tenant's lease of your property is not the tenant's homestead. No Michigan statute lets a lease waive these exemptions, and the library does not offer an exemption waiver for Michigan: a waiver of the homestead exemption would be empty for an ordinary tenant, whether a waiver of the personal property exemptions in a lease is enforceable against the Constitution is case law, and the Truth in Renting Act already voids a lease term giving you a security interest in the tenant's personal property except as law specifically allows, while the Consumer Protection Act makes an unclear waiver of a legal right unlawful. A landlord who still wants an exemption waiver should take legal advice and write its own clause.

title: Agreed Damages and Penalties in Michigan Leases
bodyText:
No Michigan statute sets a general rule on agreed (liquidated) damages in a residential lease. Michigan courts enforce an agreed sum only if it is reasonable in relation to the possible injury and is not unconscionable or excessive; otherwise it is an unenforceable penalty.

A lease may never make the tenant pay your legal costs or attorney fees beyond what a statute allows, and a security deposit may be used only for actual damage beyond normal habitation, unpaid rent (including rent due for premature termination) and unpaid utility bills, so a deposit cannot be kept as a fixed forfeit.

The only statutory liquidated damages for a tenancy are in mobile home parks: a lease or park rules may award the prevailing party up to $500 in a contested just-cause termination action in district court and up to $300 for each appeal.

The library's Michigan charges are the documented actual cost (what a third party bills you, or the price of parts or materials, with no markup and a copy of the bill), never a fixed penalty.

title: Waiving Casualty and Mitigation Rules in Michigan
bodyText: Casualty: if a leased building is destroyed or made untenantable or unfit for occupancy by the elements or any other cause without the tenant's fault or neglect, a Michigan tenant may quit and surrender possession and owes no rent after surrender, unless the parties made an express agreement to the contrary in writing. The statute therefore lets a written lease displace the surrender right, but the library does not offer that term: it would bear hardest on tenants whose homes are unlivable, a court could treat it as altering the habitability remedies no lease may waive, and your covenant of fitness still applies. The library's optional casualty clause, for leases of 1 year or more, keeps the tenant's surrender right. A lease may include a mutual release for fire or other casualty losses covered by the other party's insurance, where the policy permits the waiver and waives subrogation, to the extent of the insured party's recovery. Mitigation: a Michigan lease may not release either party from the duty to mitigate damages, and a rent-acceleration clause is allowed only if it states that the tenant may not owe the full accelerated amount because you must minimize damages and that either party may have a court decide the amount actually owed.

title: Tenant Remedies for a Landlord's Breach in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan gives a tenant these statutory remedies when you breach the lease or the law. Repairs and fitness: in an eviction for nonpayment the court deducts any rent excused by your breach of the lease or of the covenants of fitness and repair, and enters no possession judgment if your breach excused the rent; a court awarding repair costs for your failure to repair compensates the tenant's own labor at a reasonable rate. Where the Housing Law applies, rent is paid into escrow while a certificate of compliance is withheld or suspended (unless the tenant caused the hazard, and once you have had a reasonable time to apply for a temporary certificate), an occupant may sue to enforce the Housing Law, a court hearing an occupant's own enforcement suit may let that occupant fix a violation the occupant did not cause and deduct the cost from rent, and an occupant may recover actual damages after notice and your failure to correct unsafe, unsanitary or unhealthful conditions. Casualty: the tenant may surrender a home made untenantable without the tenant's fault and owe no further rent, unless agreed otherwise in writing. Possession: for a lockout or other unlawful interference the tenant recovers actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence (3 times actual damages or $200 if forcibly put out), plus possession; these rights cannot be waived. A possession judgment is also refused for retaliation. Deposits: if you do not comply fully with the return rules, you waive all claimed damages and owe double the amount retained. Lease terms: for a term the Truth in Renting Act bars, if you do not cure it within 20 days after the tenant's written notice (or at once where you actually knew), the tenant may sue to void the lease and for $250 or $500 or actual damages, and the winning party recovers costs and statutory attorney fees. Consumer practices: actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees. Source of income (landlords of 5 or more units): an injunction and actual damages, or up to 3 times the monthly rent if less, plus costs and attorney fees. Michigan's lead statute is a criminal penalty; no statute directs rent withholding for a lead hazard.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires your promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed.

An unkept promise still carries risk. The Michigan Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases and makes it unlawful to represent that something will be provided promptly or by a set time when you know or have reason to know it will not be, and to allow gross discrepancies between oral representations and the written agreement, or to fail to provide the promised benefits; a tenant who suffers loss may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees, and a lease term that violates the act is void.

A promised repair can also become a term of the lease, and the facilities you promise for the tenant's use are part of the rental unit under the security deposit act. Your covenants of fitness and repair apply whatever you promised.

Put every promise in the lease with a date, and say which items are one-time work, using the library's optional promised-work clause.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Michigan Leases
bodyText: Michigan's Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate a later dispute valid, enforceable and irrevocable, except on a ground that would let a court revoke any contract, and it has no exception for consumer contracts or residential leases. Before a dispute arises, a party may not give up the right to be represented by a lawyer in the arbitration. The library still does not offer an arbitration clause for Michigan. The Truth in Renting Act voids any lease term that waives or alters a party's right to demand a jury or any other right of notice or procedure required by law in a court case arising under the lease, or a party's rights in eviction (summary) proceedings, and a tenant may sue over such a term for $250 or $500 or actual damages, plus costs and statutory attorney fees, without first giving notice where you knew the term was unlawful. Whether a pre-dispute arbitration clause is such a term, and how federal arbitration law affects that rule, are questions of case law. Under the library's rule, a clause whose inclusion could carry a statutory penalty, or whose safety turns only on case law, is not offered. Evictions stay in district court as summary proceedings, and money claims of $7,000 or less (from January 1, 2024) can go to the small claims division. After a dispute arises, you and the tenant may still agree to arbitrate that dispute.

title: What a Michigan Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Michigan requires a written residential lease to contain: the name and address at which notices to you under the Truth in Renting Act are to be given; the Truth in Renting notice, in a prominent place in type at least 12-point (or legible print with letters at least 1/8 inch); and a provision letting a tenant who has occupied the unit for more than 13 months end the lease on 60 days' written notice on becoming eligible for subsidized senior housing or becoming unable to live independently. Depending on the lease: a condominium lease must state that the tenant will comply with the condominium documents; the lease may not put an added charge or fee on every allowed method of paying rent, so at least one allowed method (the only method, if there is just one) must carry no added charge or fee, and a lease allowing more than one method must say which method is free; a rent-acceleration clause must also state that the tenant may not owe the full accelerated amount because you must minimize damages and that either party may have a court decide the amount owed; and you may adjust terms during the lease on 30 days' written notice only for the three kinds of change the law lists. If you take a security deposit, the written deposit notice (which may be in the lease) is due within 14 days after the tenant takes possession, with its statement in 12-point boldface type at least 4 points larger than the rest. The domestic violence statement may go in the lease; if it does not, you must post or deliver it. For housing built before 1978 the federal lead disclosure applies. Michigan has no rule that the lease's start and end dates appear on its first page.

title: No Initials Requirement for Michigan Lease Notices
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires the tenant to initial or separately sign any notice or clause in a residential lease (Michigan Compiled Laws and Constitution searched). Michigan's form rules for lease texts are about type size and placement: the Truth in Renting notice in a prominent place in at least 12-point type, and the security deposit statement in 12-point boldface at least 4 points larger than the rest. Consent to electronic service of an eviction demand must be specific, in writing, and confirmed by an exchange of electronic messages; the library's optional consent clause adds a space for the tenant's initials as a drafting choice, not because a statute requires initials.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan has no plain-language law for consumer contracts or residential leases: no statute sets a readability test, requires a lease to be divided into captioned sections, or reaches leases through a consumer-contract plain-language rule (Michigan Compiled Laws and Constitution searched). Michigan's plain-language rules cover other documents, such as the small claims instruction sheets and court and friend-of-the-court materials. Specific lease texts have type rules: the Truth in Renting notice must be in a prominent place in at least 12-point type, and the security deposit and notice-of-damages statements must be in 12-point boldface at least 4 points larger than the rest. The Consumer Protection Act still matters: causing a probability of confusion or misunderstanding about a party's legal rights, obligations or remedies is an unlawful practice, and a lease term that violates the act is void, so write the lease clearly.

title: No Consumer Restrictions Statement in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan has no statute requiring a residential lease to carry a front-page statement listing the tenant's waivers or consumer restrictions, a readability test, or attorney general pre-approval (Michigan Compiled Laws and Constitution searched). The closest Michigan rule is the Truth in Renting notice every lease must print in a prominent place, telling the tenant that Michigan law establishes rights and obligations for the parties and that the tenant may want legal help with a question about a provision. Because the Truth in Renting Act voids lease waivers of the tenant's main statutory protections, and the Consumer Protection Act allows a waiver of a legal right only if it is clearly stated and specifically consented to, the library's Michigan leases include no waivers to list.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing in Michigan
Lease Length and Formalities in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan sets no maximum term for a private residential lease and no special formality such as a seal or acknowledgment. A lease for a longer period than 1 year is void unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party making the lease (you) or by an agent authorized in writing; a lease of 1 year or less need not be in writing. No Michigan statute requires a married owner's spouse to join in or consent to a lease (Michigan's 1947 community property act was repealed in 1948). The length of the term matters elsewhere: you and the tenant may modify your repair covenants only where the lease has a current term of at least 1 year, and the library's casualty-termination and tenant-repair clauses are offered only for terms of at least 1 year. Condominium conversions give some tenants a right to an extended lease, which this library does not cover.

title: Optional Lease Terms Michigan Allows
bodyText: Michigan law lets a lease add or choose these terms, and the library offers each one it uses as an optional clause: modifying your repair covenants by having the tenant take on specified repairs, only in a lease with a current term of at least 1 year; a landlord casualty-termination right for terms of at least 1 year, keeping the tenant's statutory surrender right; rent acceleration after breach, with the mitigation statement the law requires; rent increases during the term on at least 30 days' written notice to cover increases in property taxes, listed utility charges or listed insurance premiums; termination for controlled-substance activity, which supports a 24-hour notice to quit after a police report; consent to electronic service of an eviction demand; authorizing housing inspectors to enter where the Housing Law applies; the domestic violence statement; a shorter period for returning the move-in checklist; and a mutual release for fire or casualty losses covered by the other party's insurance, which the library does not offer because for the tenant it is a waiver that must be clearly stated and specifically consented to. A lease with an option to purchase a 1-to-4-unit home makes you a seller under the Seller Disclosure Act: you must deliver the state seller's disclosure statement before signing and indicate compliance on the lease, an addendum or a separate document. Money paid for the option is not a security deposit unless it was meant to evade the deposit law. Michigan has no rent-to-own statute of its own (Michigan Compiled Laws searched), and the library offers no option-to-purchase clause.

title: Disclosures Michigan Requires for a Rental
bodyText: Michigan requires these written disclosures for a residential rental. In the lease: your name and address for notices under the Truth in Renting Act and the Truth in Renting notice; the senior-housing and infirmity termination right; for a condominium unit, the tenant's duty to comply with the condominium documents; and at least one allowed way to pay rent (the only one, if there is just one) that carries no added fee, named as such if more than one way is allowed. In the lease or separately: the domestic violence release statement, or else a posted or delivered notice with the same words when the lease is signed. If you take a security deposit: the written deposit notice within 14 days after move-in (your name and address, where the deposit is held, and the 4-day forwarding-address statement in large boldface type), two blank move-in inventory checklists with their required heading, and at move-out the itemized notice of damages with its 7-day response statement. For pre-1978 housing: the federal lead-based paint disclosure. For a lease with an option to purchase a 1-to-4-unit home: the state seller's disclosure statement before signing, with compliance indicated on the lease, an addendum or a separate document. Where the Housing Law applies, you must tell the tenant when the enforcing agency asks to inspect. Michigan has no notice of rent-regulation or just-cause coverage (local rent control is barred by state law), no state form that must be the lease's first page, and no sale-leaseback warning. A real estate licensee helping with a lease of 1 to 4 units must give the agency-relationship disclosure.

title: Preset Cleaning and Repair Charges
bodyText: No Michigan statute lets a lease set a schedule of preset cleaning, carpet or repair charges, requires a special notice for one, or sets a professional-cleaning rule. The security deposit statute itself limits what you may take, and a lease cannot waive it. A deposit may be used only to reimburse you for actual damages to the rental unit or any ancillary facility that are the direct result of conduct not reasonably expected in the normal course of living in a dwelling, and to pay rent in arrears, rent due because the tenant ended the lease early, and utility bills the tenant did not pay. Within 30 days after the tenant's occupancy ends, your notice of damages must itemize each damaged item with its estimated cost of repair and the amounts and bases of each charge, and it may not include damage that was claimed on a termination inventory checklist before this tenant moved in. A preset charge deducted whether or not the damage occurred, or a charge for the ordinary cleaning that normal living requires, would claim more than those uses allow and could be read as a waiver of the tenant's deposit rights, which a Michigan lease may not contain. So the library offers no preset-charge clause for Michigan: charge each item at its actual repair cost in the itemized notice of damages, and use the move-in and move-out inventory checklists the statute requires to show the condition. These rules cover every rental unit used as a home, including apartments, rooming and boarding houses, mobile home spaces and single and 2-family dwellings.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: No Michigan statute gives a tenant a right to pay a security deposit in installments or requires you to offer a payment plan. You may agree to one. If you do, put the amounts and due dates in the lease, because once the lease starts you may not change its terms without the tenant's written consent. Each installment is part of the security deposit: the total you require may not exceed 1 1/2 months' rent, every installment must be deposited in a regulated financial institution (unless you have posted the bond the statute allows), and you may not require a deposit at all unless you give the written deposit notice no later than 14 days after the tenant takes possession. The Public Service Commission's rule that a regulated electric or gas utility must let an eligible low-income customer pay a utility deposit in 2 monthly installments applies to the utility's own deposit, not to a landlord.

title: Forwarding Address and Move-Out Conditions
bodyText: No Michigan statute lets you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving notice of moving out or returning keys, and none requires such notice for a refund. What Michigan does have is a forwarding-address rule. Your written deposit notice must tell the tenant to give you, in writing and within 4 days after moving out, a forwarding address where the tenant can receive mail. If the tenant does not, you are relieved of sending the notice of damages, and you may keep the amount you claim without first getting a court judgment, but the tenant's later claim for the deposit is not lost. If you leave the forwarding-address statement out of your deposit notice, the tenant is relieved of that duty. Your own deadlines run from the end of the tenant's occupancy: mail any notice of damages within 30 days, and, if the tenant disputes it in time, sue for the disputed amount within 45 days or return it. Any other move-out condition, such as forfeiting the deposit for missing keys or a missed notice to vacate, would add a ground of forfeiture the deposit statute does not allow and could be read as a waiver of the tenant's deposit rights. Rent the tenant owes because a periodic tenancy was not properly ended, or for early termination, may be taken from the deposit and itemized like any other charge.

title: No Deposit-Standards Posting Rule
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires you to post, or give applicants, the standards you use to set security deposit amounts, whatever the number of units you own, or to use one standard for every unit. Two rules limit how you set deposits. The total deposit may not exceed 1 1/2 months' rent. And a landlord of 5 or more rental units in Michigan, counting related entities, may not make any distinction in the price, terms, conditions, fees or privileges of a rental because of a prospective or current tenant's source of income, such as a housing voucher or other assistance; Michigan's civil rights acts also bar different terms for protected classes (edu-fair-housing-mi). Keeping written deposit standards and applying them the same way to every applicant is the practical way to show compliance.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: No Michigan statute sets up a procedure for a tenant to ask for an early or expedited deposit decision, or a fee for one. You may always return a deposit sooner than the law requires. The statutory timetable runs from the end of the tenant's occupancy: within 30 days, mail the notice of damages with a check or money order for the balance, or, from September 21, 2026, send the balance by direct deposit or electronic transfer within 10 days after mailing the notice. If you miss the 30 days, you are treated as agreeing that no damages are due and must return the full deposit immediately. If the tenant disputes your claim in time, you have 45 days after occupancy ends to start a court action for the disputed amount or return it. A domestic violence release does not entitle the tenant to an early refund: you may still withhold for unpaid rent as the statute allows. Any fee for faster handling would itself be a charge against deposit rights the lease cannot add.

title: No Rule on Fees in Lieu of a Deposit
bodyText: No Michigan statute regulates a fee charged in place of a security deposit or a deposit-alternative or surety program, requires you to offer one to every applicant, gives the tenant a right to switch to a regular deposit, or requires a notice before a damage claim under such a program is reported to a credit bureau or collector. The deposit statute decides how the money is treated. A security deposit is any deposit, in any amount, the tenant pays you to be held for the term or part of it, and any other money returnable to the tenant on condition that the unit is returned in the condition the lease requires. So if any part of what the tenant pays under the program is held, credited back or refunded depending on the unit's condition, treat that part as a security deposit: it counts toward the 1 1/2-month limit and must be held, noticed, used and returned under the deposit rules. A flat fee that is never held or returned is most likely a fee rather than a deposit, but no Michigan statute or case the library has read settles that; the cautious course is to keep any such fee plus any deposit within 1 1/2 months' rent. The fee does not reduce what the tenant owes for damage. If you offer the program, state the fee, what it buys and what it does not (for example, that the tenant remains liable for damage and unpaid rent), so the lease does not mislead under the Consumer Protection Act. If you, counting related entities, own 5 or more rental units in Michigan, offer the same choice on the same terms whatever the tenant's source of income. The insurer or surety behind a program is regulated by the Insurance Code.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: No Michigan statute governs holding deposits, reservation fees or earnest money taken before a lease is signed, and none makes you return a holding deposit doubled if you back out. The deposit statute defines a security deposit as money the tenant pays to be held for the term of the rental agreement, and it excludes prepayment of the first full rental period. Whether money paid before there is a lease or a tenant in possession is a security deposit is not settled by the statute. The cautious course: take a holding deposit only under a short written agreement that says what it is for, when it is credited, when it is refunded and when it is kept; at signing, credit it to the first month's rent, or treat it as part of the security deposit, counting it toward the 1 1/2-month limit and giving the written deposit notice within 14 days after the tenant takes possession. If the arrangement ends under its own terms, for example because you decline the application, return the money promptly: failing to promptly restore a deposit or other payment when a consumer transaction is canceled or terminated under its terms is an unfair practice under the Consumer Protection Act. If you own 5 or more rental units, you may not treat an applicant differently in fees or terms because of the applicant's source of income.

title: Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees
bodyText: Michigan has no rule on nonrefundable deposits and no notice for making part of a deposit nonrefundable, and the label does not decide the question. A security deposit is any deposit, in any amount, the tenant pays you to be held for the term, including any required prepayment of rent other than the first full rental period, any rent charged for a period above the average rent for the term, and any other money returnable to the tenant on condition that the unit is returned in the condition the lease requires. Money you hold to secure the tenant's performance or against damage is therefore a security deposit even if the lease calls it nonrefundable: it counts toward the 1 1/2-month limit, must be held, noticed, used and returned under the deposit rules, and a term making it nonrefundable would waive deposit rights and be void. A fee charged for something specific, such as a nonrefundable pet fee, that you do not hold as security and that is not returnable, is a fee and not a deposit. State each nonrefundable fee in the lease with its amount and what it is for, never call security money a fee, and keep the fees out of anything you describe as a deposit. In a mobile home park, the owner may not charge an entrance fee or a refundable or nonrefundable exit fee.

title: Nonrefundable Fees: No Separate Notice Rule
bodyText: Michigan does not require a separate document, a special form, bold type or the tenant's initials to make a fee nonrefundable, because Michigan has no category of nonrefundable deposit. No form of words can make a security deposit nonrefundable: money held to secure the tenant's performance or against damage stays a security deposit and must be returned under the deposit rules, whatever the lease calls it. The deposit statute's formatting rules are for other notices: the forwarding-address statement in your written deposit notice, the statement at the top of the inventory checklist, and the statement in the notice of damages, each in 12-point boldface type. State each true nonrefundable fee, with its amount and purpose, in the lease (edu-nonrefundable-deposit-notice-mi).

title: Michigan Money Limits for Rentals
bodyText: Michigan sets few money limits on residential rentals. No statute caps rent, late fees, application or screening fees, pet fees or other lease charges, and local governments may not control the amount of rent. The limits that do apply: Security deposit: no more than 1 1/2 months' rent in total, counting a refundable pet deposit and any required prepayment of rent other than the first full rental period. Payment methods: a lease may not put an added charge or fee on every allowed way to pay rent, so at least one allowed method (the only one, if there is just one) must be fee-free. Attorney fees and court costs: a lease may not make a party pay the other's legal costs or attorney fees beyond what a statute specifically allows; in an eviction case the court may add only limited taxable costs ($75 for a motion resulting in dismissal or judgment, or for a default or consent judgment, and $150 for a trial) to the costs allowed in other civil actions. Bounced checks: after the statutory written demand, a $25 processing fee if the maker pays within 7 days (excluding weekends and holidays) or $35 within 30 days; if unpaid, a court may award the check amount, civil damages of 2 times the check or $100, whichever is greater, and $250 costs. Interest: the legal rate is 5% a year, and a written agreement may set up to 7% a year. Mobile home parks: no entrance fee and no refundable or nonrefundable exit fee; a lease may provide liquidated damages to the prevailing party in a contested just-cause termination of no more than $500 in the district court and $300 for each appeal level. Housing Law inspections: where the Housing Law applies, the enforcing agency's inspection fee may not exceed the actual, reasonable cost of the inspection. Penalties you can owe: double the security deposit retained for failing to follow the return rules; $250 or $500 (or actual damages) under the Truth in Renting Act; actual damages or $200 per occurrence for unlawful interference with possession, 3 times damages for a forcible eviction; and, for source-of-income discrimination by a landlord of 5 or more units, actual damages or up to 3 times the monthly rent, whichever is less, with costs and attorney fees.

title: Listing Fees in the Lease
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires the lease to list every fee, to state rent and required fees as one total, or to bar a fee for common-area maintenance.

Two rules make a complete list the safe practice. Once the lease begins, you may not add a fee or change one without the tenant's written consent, except for the three adjustments a lease may provide for on at least 30 days' written notice (changes required by law, rule changes needed for health, safety or peaceful enjoyment, and rent changes to cover increases in property taxes, listed utility charges or certain insurance premiums). And under the Consumer Protection Act, failing to reveal a material fact the tenant could not reasonably know, or a gross discrepancy between what you said and what the written lease says, is unlawful.

At least one allowed way to pay rent (the only one, if there is just one) must be fee-free.

In a mobile home park the owner may not charge an entrance fee or an exit fee, and may charge for electric, fuel or water service only if each resident's use is accurately measured, unless the service is included in the rent. The library's Fees and Charges clause lists every fee in one place.

When you list fees, do not list attorney fees or legal, court, eviction or collection costs: a lease may not make the tenant liable for legal costs or attorney fees beyond those a statute specifically permits. The library's cautious course is also to list no fixed charge for a breach of the lease, and to charge for damage or a third-party service only the documented actual cost. Do not list a fee that applies to every allowed way of paying rent. Any refundable deposit you list, such as a pet or key deposit, is part of the security deposit, and all deposits together may not exceed 1 1/2 months' rent.

title: Passing Government Fines to a Tenant
bodyText:
No Michigan statute bars you from making a tenant reimburse a fine, penalty or abatement charge a government imposes on you, and none makes a tenant liable to you for one by default. Whether a tenant who caused the violation owes the fine to you without a lease term is case law, so put any reimbursement in the lease, at the amount you actually paid, shown by a copy of the citation, order or bill.

Your own duties limit what you can pass on. You covenant that the premises and common areas are fit for their intended use and that you will keep them in reasonable repair and comply with state and local health and safety laws, except where the disrepair or violation was caused by the tenant's wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct; a lease may modify those covenants only if its current term is at least 1 year, and may not waive or alter the tenant's remedies for their breach.

So a fine for a code violation you are responsible for stays with you.

Where the Housing Law applies, the code works the same way: rent escrow for an uncertified building does not apply if you show the hazard was caused by the occupants, and a court that finds the occupant caused a violation may let you correct it and charge the cost to the occupant or the occupant's security deposit.

The library's optional clause (tenant-caused-fines-as) covers only fines and abatement charges for conditions the tenant, the household or the tenant's guests caused or permitted, and never one you are responsible for.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: No Michigan statute addresses passing a government fee, such as a rental registration, license or inspection fee, on to a tenant. Where the Housing Law applies, the local enforcing agency may charge a reasonable inspection fee that may not exceed the actual, reasonable cost of the inspection, and you are not liable for it if the agency is the direct cause of an inspection not being performed. Many cities, including Detroit, Grand Rapids, Ann Arbor and Lansing, run their own registration and inspection programs, which this library does not cover. How you recover the cost is limited by the Truth in Renting Act. Once a lease begins you may not add a charge or raise the rent without the tenant's written consent, except for adjustments the lease provides for on at least 30 days' written notice: changes required by law, rule changes needed for health, safety or peaceful enjoyment, and rent changes to cover increases in property taxes, charges for electricity, heating fuel, water or sewer service consumed at the property, or liability, fire or worker compensation insurance premiums. A registration or inspection fee is not on that list, and a fee charged to you is not a change in the lease that the law requires. So build a known government fee into the rent, or state it as a fixed charge in the lease when it is signed; a later increase can be recovered only at renewal or by agreement. The library offers no pass-through clause for Michigan.

title: Charges for Alarm Tampering
bodyText:
No Michigan statute authorizes, sets or caps a fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and none makes tampering by a tenant an offense.

The duties run mostly to you. Where the Housing Law applies, each unit in a Class A multiple dwelling must have a smoke alarm meeting the construction code, and violating that is a misdemeanor. Under the residential code for smoke alarms in homes built before November 6, 1974, the owner is responsible for proper operation, testing and maintenance, the occupant of a rental unit must periodically test and clean the alarms as the manufacturer's instructions say, and a failed alarm must be repaired and working within 30 days.

What you may charge a tenant is set by general rules. Your repair covenant does not cover disrepair caused by the tenant's wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct, so a tenant who disables or damages an alarm that way can be charged for the repair; the security deposit covers actual damage from conduct not reasonably expected in normal living. A fixed tampering fee above your real cost would be tested by the courts' rule that an agreed charge must be reasonable in relation to the possible injury, so the library's optional clause (detector-care-mi) charges only the documented cost of repair or replacement.

Some cities add alarm rules by ordinance.

title: No Carpet-Cleaning Statute
bodyText: No Michigan statute lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, sets a condition for doing so (such as cleaning before the tenancy), or limits carpet or paint deductions by the carpet's age or condition. The deposit statute decides what you can charge. A security deposit may be used only for actual damages to the unit that are the direct result of conduct not reasonably expected in the normal course of living in a dwelling, and for unpaid rent and utility bills. Ordinary soil and wear from normal living are not that kind of damage, so routine carpet cleaning cannot be taken from the deposit, and a lease term saying it can would waive the tenant's deposit rights and be void. Stains, burns, pet damage or other damage beyond normal living can be charged at the actual cost of cleaning, repair or replacement, itemized in the notice of damages within 30 days after occupancy ends. Record carpet condition on the move-in and move-out inventory checklists the statute requires (carpeting is one of the listed items), because those are your evidence. The library offers no carpet-cleaning clause for Michigan.

title: Collection Fees
bodyText: No Michigan statute authorizes or caps a collection fee a landlord adds to past-due rent or other lease charges. Several rules limit one. A Michigan lease may not make the tenant pay your legal costs or attorney fees in a dispute under the lease beyond what a statute specifically allows. A licensed collection agency may not collect a fee from the tenant for collecting a claim, other than a claim owed to you under the original agreement, so an agency can add a collection charge only if the lease itself provides for one, and it may not share in an attorney's fee or misstate the debtor's legal rights. Michigan's collection-practices act also bars businesses collecting their own debts from misleading or harassing debtors; whether it covers rent is not settled by its text. An agreed collection charge would be tested by the courts' rule that an agreed charge for a breach must be reasonable in relation to the possible injury, and a charge for collecting a disputed amount risks being treated as a barred legal cost. The library therefore offers no collection-fee clause for Michigan; recover collection costs through the court costs a statute allows, and the landlord may add its own clause.

title: No Notice-Service Fee
bodyText: No Michigan statute authorizes a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice, such as a demand for possession or a notice to quit, or for filing an eviction. The Truth in Renting Act limits one: a lease may not make the tenant liable for your legal costs or attorney fees in a dispute under the lease beyond what a statute specifically allows, and may not waive or alter the tenant's rights in summary proceedings. In a possession case the court may award the costs allowed in other civil actions in that court plus limited extra amounts ($75 for a motion resulting in dismissal or judgment, or for a default or consent judgment, and $150 for a trial), and only those costs; it takes into account any rent it finds excused by your breach. A notice or eviction-filing fee in the lease would add to those costs and would also be tested by the courts' rule that an agreed charge for a breach must be reasonable in relation to the possible injury. The library therefore offers no notice-service fee for Michigan; recover service and filing costs through the court's cost award. The one statutory exception is in mobile home parks, where a lease or park rule may provide liquidated damages of up to $500 in the district court and $300 for each appeal level to the party who wins a contested just-cause termination.

title: Late Fees in Subsidized Tenancies
bodyText: Michigan has no late-fee rule written for subsidized or voucher tenancies, and no general late-fee cap. Two Michigan rules and the federal program rules shape what you may charge. If you, with related entities, are a landlord of 5 or more rental units in Michigan, you may not make any distinction in the price, terms, conditions, fees or privileges of a rental because of a tenant's source of income, which includes housing assistance and housing choice vouchers, and you may not treat a tenant differently for using emergency rental assistance; the civil rights act's version of that rule has narrow exceptions for owner-occupied 2-family homes and rooms in the owner's home. Charging a voucher tenant a late fee because the housing agency paid its share late, or a different late fee than other tenants pay, risks violating that rule. Under the federal voucher program the family is not responsible for the housing agency's share of the rent, the agency's failure to pay that share is not a lease violation by the tenant, and you may not end the tenancy during the lease term for the agency's nonpayment. The voucher contract between you and the agency provides for late-payment penalties against the agency in some cases, and only if you also charge tenants late fees for late payment of their own share. The cautious course is to charge a late fee only when the tenant's own share is late, figured on that share. If you take rent through the Department of Health and Human Services rent vendoring program, you may not evict an occupant solely because the department ended your participation for a code violation or unpaid property taxes.

title: Passing Tax and Insurance Increases to Tenants
bodyText:
A Michigan lease may pass increases in property taxes to the tenant during the term, but only as a rent change the lease provides for, made on at least 30 days' written notice, to cover additional operating costs you incur because of increases in ad valorem property taxes, in charges for electricity, heating fuel, water or sanitary sewer service consumed at the property, or in premiums for liability, fire or worker compensation insurance.

Without such a provision you may not raise the rent or add a charge during the term without the tenant's written consent.

No Michigan statute requires the clause to state the tenant's exact share, or to refund a share of a later tax abatement, and the deposit statute has no tax-share deduction. Stating how the increase is figured, allocating only the property's share, and crediting any later reduction keep the increase to the additional costs the statute allows. Other insurance premiums, such as property coverage beyond fire, and other taxes or fees are not on the list. The library's optional clause for this is rent-cost-adjustment-mi.

title: No Rule Tying Rent to the Repair Duty
bodyText: Michigan has no statute like the uniform landlord-tenant act's rule that a lease, assignment, deed or security instrument may not let anyone receive rent free of the duty to maintain the premises; the Michigan Compiled Laws, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws and the Public Service Commission billing rules were searched, and Michigan did not adopt that uniform act. What Michigan law does say: in every lease or license of residential premises the lessor or licensor covenants that the premises and common areas are fit for their intended use and will be kept in reasonable repair and in compliance with health and safety laws, so whoever leases the unit to the tenant carries those duties, and a lease may not waive or alter the tenant's remedies when the premises are unfit. If your lender enforces an assignment of rents and collects rent from your tenant, it need not spend the rent on maintenance, but its right to collect is subject to the lease and to the tenant's claims and defenses from your nonperformance unless the tenant made an enforceable agreement not to assert them, and the tenant may ask a court to appoint a receiver if the unpaid maintenance threatens the tenant's interest. Where the Housing Law applies, a court-appointed receiver may collect the rents ahead of prior assignees and apply them to bringing the building into compliance.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Michigan has no opt-in lockout for unpaid rent, and a lease cannot create one. Any tenant in possession whose possessory interest you unlawfully interfere with may recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence, and possession if it was lost. Unlawful interference includes changing, altering or adding to the locks or other security devices without immediately giving the tenant keys, removing doors, windows or locks, boarding up the premises, removing or keeping the tenant's belongings, and cutting off an essential service you must furnish or the tenant procured. A tenant put out by force may recover 3 times actual damages or $200, whichever is greater. These rights cannot be waived, and a lease term that waives or alters them is void. You may retake the unit without a court only in narrow cases: under a court order; temporarily to make repairs or inspections as the law allows; after a good-faith belief, after diligent inquiry, that the tenant has abandoned the unit and current rent is unpaid; or under the statute's procedure after a sole tenant's death. A lease also may not give you a security interest in the tenant's belongings to secure rent, except as the law allows. For unpaid rent, serve a written demand for possession; if the tenant neither pays nor leaves within 7 days after service, file summary proceedings, and the court officer carries out any order of eviction (edu-self-help-eviction-mi).

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: Michigan has no separate rule for a utility deposit a landlord holds. Money you collect from a tenant that is returnable when the unit is returned in the required condition, including money held against utility bills, is a security deposit: it counts toward the 1 1/2-month limit and must be held, noticed and returned under the deposit rules. The deposit may be used to pay utility bills the tenant did not pay, along with unpaid rent and actual damage, and any amount you keep must be itemized in the notice of damages mailed within 30 days after occupancy ends, with the balance returned. A deposit an electric or gas utility regulated by the Public Service Commission takes from your tenant is governed by the commission's rules, not by you: the utility may require one only in listed situations, must pay 5% annual interest, must return the deposit with interest after 12 consecutive months of satisfactory payment (36 months where the deposit was assessed for unauthorized use), credits it to the final bill when service ends and promptly returns any balance, gives a receipt, and must offer an eligible low-income customer 2 monthly installments. Municipal utilities are outside those rules. A tenant who is not served under a lease that includes utilities must open an account with the utility within 30 business days of taking occupancy (edu-utility-landlord-account-mi).

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText:
No Michigan statute regulates rent concessions, free-rent periods or move-in specials as such. Two general rules shape how to give one.

First, the deposit statute counts as a security deposit any sum required to be paid as rent in a rental period in excess of the average rent for the term. A concession that makes some months cheaper than others, such as a free last month, makes the other months' rent higher than the average, and the statute's words treat the excess as a security deposit, which counts toward the 1 1/2-month limit and must be held and returned under the deposit rules. The cautious course is to spread the concession evenly as the same reduction in every full rental period, so no month exceeds the average.

Second, under the Consumer Protection Act it is unlawful to represent that a tenant will receive a rebate, discount or other benefit as an inducement to sign if the benefit depends on an event after signing, or to advertise something as free without clearly disclosing its conditions. So make a concession unconditional once the lease is signed, and do not take it back if the tenant leaves early: recapture would also be tested as a penalty and, if it accelerates rent, must carry the statutory mitigation statement.

State each concession in the lease; the library's optional clause is rent-concession-mi.

title: Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Michigan does not tax ordinary residential rent. Its use tax reaches rooms or lodging furnished by hotels, motels and others offering accommodations to the public, including inns, tourist homes, lodging houses, rooming houses and apartment hotels, but not rooms and lodging rented for a continuous period of more than 1 month; the rate is 6%. So a rooming-house or furnished room rented by the night or week to the public can be taxable, while a lease of a home or apartment for more than a month is not. Counties and other local bodies may also levy accommodations or convention and tourism taxes on rooms provided to transient guests, defined as people staying less than 30 consecutive days, and the Accommodations Tax Act lets certain counties levy up to 5% of the total charge, or up to 8% with voter approval. No Michigan statute addresses passing a repealed local tax through to tenants. If you rent short-term or furnish rooms to the public, check the use tax and any local accommodations ordinance before setting your rates; this library does not cover local ordinances.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule
bodyText: Michigan has no state rent-reporting program, does not require any landlord to offer tenants positive rent reporting, and does not bar you from offering it. The 2026 act limiting purchases of single-family homes by large institutional investors mentions positive rent reporting only as one condition of certain purchases exempt from its ban, not as a duty on landlords. One Michigan notice rule can apply when a lease has a cosigner. Before reporting adverse information about a cosigner to a credit bureau, giving the cosigner's obligation to a collection agency or taking collection action against the cosigner, the creditor must mail the cosigner a first-class notice that the primary obligor is delinquent and that the cosigner is responsible, and give the cosigner at least 30 days to pay or make other satisfactory arrangements; a cosigner who does so may not be reported. The rule does not cover a person who signed a guarantee, and whether a lease obligation is the kind of household indebtedness the act covers is not settled, so the cautious course is to give the notice. A cosigner who suffers loss may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees. A licensed collection agency may not publish lists of debtors except for credit reporting in response to a prospective creditor's specific inquiry.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No Michigan statute specifically bars charging a tenant a fee for a service you do not actually provide. General rules still make it unlawful in practice. Michigan's Consumer Protection Act covers residential leasing, and its unfair practices include a failure to provide the promised benefits, gross differences between what you said and what the lease says, representing that services have benefits they do not have, and charging a price grossly above what similar services sell for. A lease term that violates the act is void, and a tenant who suffers loss may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees. A fee for a service the lease promises is also part of the bargain: if you stop providing it, that is your breach of the lease, and in a possession case for nonpayment the court deducts rent it finds excused by your breach. In a mobile home park, the owner may not charge for electric, fuel or water service unless the resident's use is accurately and consistently measured, or the service is included in the rent. Charge only for services you actually provide, and say in the lease what happens to the fee if the service stops.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText:
No Michigan statute caps or sets a formula for late fees on a residential lease. The figure is your own, stated in the lease (the library's Late Fee clause).

The limit comes from the courts: Michigan courts enforce an agreed charge for a breach only if it is reasonable in relation to the possible injury and not unconscionable or excessive. Keep the fee to a reasonable estimate of what a late payment costs you, and charge it once per late payment, not daily without limit.

Several related rules apply. A lease may not let you raise the late fee mid-term without the tenant's written consent. At least one allowed way to pay rent (the only one, if there is just one) must be free of any added charge or fee. The library's Michigan default clause does not end the lease or evict for an unpaid late fee alone, because whether a late fee is rent due for a nonpayment demand is unsettled.

In a mobile home park there is no late-fee cap either, but 3 or more late payments in 12 months, each followed by a written demand for possession that the tenant did not pay within the time stated, is just cause to end the tenancy, and each demand must carry the statement: Notice: Three or more late payments of rent during any 12-month period is just cause to evict you.

The Public Service Commission's 2% cap on late payment charges applies to regulated utilities, not landlords.

title: Deposits After a Domestic Violence Release
bodyText: Michigan has no special deposit deadline for a tenant released from rent under its domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking statute (`edu-dv-release-mi`), and no rule saying the deposit clock waits until every occupant has moved out (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The ordinary deposit rules apply (`security-deposit-return-mi`): within 30 days after the tenant's occupancy ends you must mail any notice of damages with its itemized list and the balance (or send the balance electronically within 10 days after mailing the notice), and within 45 days you must either sue for the damages claimed or return the balance; the tenant must give you a forwarding address in writing within 4 days after moving out. The release statute (which covers leases entered into, renewed or renegotiated after October 5, 2010) adds three money rules. The tenant is released from rent no later than the first day of the second month that rent is due after the notice, and never before moving out, so rent is owed only up to that date. Prepaid amounts, including first and last months' rent, are not refunded. And you may still keep deposit money for accrued and unpaid rent for a rental period, or part of one, during which the tenant had actual or constructive possession, as well as other sums the deposit law lets you withhold by its usual procedure; rent for any period after the release has taken effect is not owed and can't be taken from the deposit. If other tenants on the lease stay, they remain bound by it. The deposit law runs its deadlines from the end of occupancy and does not say whether one co-tenant's move-out starts them, and no case law was read. The cautious course: tell the departing tenant in writing, at the forwarding address given, that the deposit stays with the continuing tenancy and will be accounted for when that occupancy ends, unless all the tenants agree in writing to divide it now; send that written notice within 30 days after the departing tenant moves out, and if you claim any damage or unpaid rent from that tenant, also mail an itemized notice of damages within the same 30 days; and never reveal that address to the person the tenant named as the source of danger (`edu-dv-confidentiality-mi`).

title: Evicting a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: No Michigan statute bars you from evicting a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or gives a victim a separate defense in an eviction case (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Three Michigan rules still protect victims in practice. (1) The 7-day notice to quit for a tenant, household member or person under the tenant's control who caused or threatened physical injury to someone on your property (available only after the police have been notified) does not apply when the person injured or threatened is the tenant or a member of the tenant's household, or where using it would violate federal housing regulations; the library's criminal-activity clause carries the same carve-out (`criminal-activity-mi`). (2) A court may not enter a judgment for possession if the termination was intended primarily as a penalty for the tenant's attempt to secure or enforce rights under the lease or under state or federal law, which includes the domestic violence release right (`edu-retaliation-mi`). (3) A tenant who uses the release right (`edu-dv-release-mi`) stops owing rent once the release takes effect, and the other tenants on the lease stay bound, so the release is not a default you can evict the others for. Ordinary grounds (unpaid rent, a lease breach, holding over after a proper notice) otherwise apply with no victim exception, so base any case on conduct independent of the abuse and keep a record showing it. Federal law goes further for housing in a covered program, including public housing, Housing Choice Vouchers and low-income housing tax credit units: you may not deny, terminate or evict a tenant because the tenant is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking; an incident of actual or threatened abuse is not a serious or repeated lease violation by the victim or good cause to end the victim's tenancy; you may not end a tenancy solely for abuse-related crime by a household member or guest when the tenant or an affiliated individual is the victim; and you may split the lease to remove only the abuser. A court may also order the abuser to stay out of the home under a personal protection order (`edu-dv-protection-order-chapter-moved-mi`).

title: Lock Changes for Domestic Violence Victims
bodyText: No Michigan statute gives a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking a right to have the locks changed, requires you to change them, says who pays, or voids a lease term on the subject (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Three Michigan rules bear on a request. (1) The lockout statute: changing, altering or adding to the locks or other security devices without immediately giving keys or other unlocking devices to the person in possession is an unlawful interference with a tenant's possession, for which the tenant may recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence, and possession; it is not unlawful if you act under a court order, and the rule can't be waived (`edu-self-help-eviction-mi`). So rekeying at a victim's request is safe as long as every tenant in possession gets a key. (2) Personal protection orders: a family court may order an abuser not to enter the premises (in a domestic-relationship order it may not do so against someone who is not the petitioner's spouse and has a property interest in the premises when the petitioner has none), and a stalking or sexual-assault order may bar the respondent from entering or remaining on property the petitioner owns, leases or occupies. The order binds the restrained person, not you, and Michigan law does not say whether rekeying to keep a restrained co-tenant out is acting under a court order; no case law was read. The cautious course: when a tenant gives you an order that bars another person from entering the home, rekey promptly at the tenant's request and don't give the restrained person a key; if that person is also a tenant on the lease, act only under an order that deals with that person's possession of the home or with that tenant's written agreement, or get legal advice before withholding a key. (3) Cost: no statute says who pays. Charge no more than your actual cost, as the library's keys clause provides (`keys`). A crime victim may apply to the state crime victim compensation program, which can pay up to $1,000 per residence for installing, increasing or replacing residential security, including replacing or repairing locks. In federally assisted housing, federal law protects victims from eviction because of the abuse and lets you split the lease to remove only the abuser (`edu-dv-eviction-protection-mi`).

title: Protection Order Citations in Michigan
bodyText: Nothing has moved. Michigan's domestic violence release statute (`edu-dv-release-mi`, `edu-dv-qualifying-documents-mi`) points to other laws for its documents and definitions, and as of November 13, 2026 every one of those cross-references leads to a section that exists and still says what the statute relies on. Personal protection orders are issued by the family division of circuit court under two sections of the Revised Judicature Act: one for a spouse or former spouse, a person with whom the petitioner has a child, a dating partner or a past or present household member, and one for stalking and sexual assault (Michigan Compiled Laws sections 600.2950 and 600.2950a, last amended in 2018). The release statute's reference to section 600.2950h defines only a foreign protection order (an order from another state, an Indian tribe or a U.S. territory), which also counts; a Michigan personal protection order counts under the two sections above. An order removing an abuser from a child's home is still issued under subsection (4) of the juvenile code's section 712A.13a. The definitions the release statute borrows are current: domestic violence (the Domestic Violence Prevention and Treatment Act, amended in 2023), stalking and aggravated stalking (the Penal Code, amended in 2023) and sexual assault (the criminal sexual conduct sections). No 2025 or 2026 act changes any of them. The practical point: accept any of these orders if it is still in effect on the day the tenant gives it to you, and don't rely on form language that lists section numbers instead of the statute's own words. A personal protection order is effective and enforceable anywhere in Michigan once a judge signs it, and police enforce it; if a tenant shows you one that bars another person from the home, follow its terms (`edu-no-dv-lockchange-mi`).

title: Documents for a Domestic Violence Release
bodyText: Michigan has one domestic violence rental right, the release from rent (`edu-dv-release-mi`), so it has one list of qualifying documents; there is no separate list for lock changes or eviction defenses, because Michigan has neither (`edu-no-dv-lockchange-mi`, `edu-dv-eviction-protection-mi`). The statute covers leases entered into, renewed or renegotiated after October 5, 2010. To be released, the tenant sends you, by certified mail, a written notice of intent to seek a release, a written statement that the tenant or the tenant's child has a reasonable apprehension of present danger from domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, and one or more of these documents: (a) a valid personal protection order, a foreign protection order, or a juvenile court order removing an abusive person from the home, still in effect on the date the tenant submits it; (b) a valid probation, conditional release or parole order still in effect on that date that puts the offender under conditions reasonably necessary to protect the tenant or child, such as no contact; (c) a written police report that has led the prosecuting attorney to file charges, if the charges were filed not more than 14 days before the tenant's notice; (d) such a police report with charges filed more than 14 days before the notice, but then the tenant must also demonstrate a verifiable threat of present danger, and filing the third-party report in (e) is that demonstration; or (e) a report in substantially the statutory form, signed by the tenant under penalty of perjury and verified by a qualified third party: a sexual assault or domestic violence counselor, a licensed or registered health professional, a mental health professional, or a member of the clergy affiliated with a tax-exempt religious institution. The time limits run differently: an order must be in effect on the day it is submitted, whatever its age, while the 14-day limit for a police report runs from the filing of charges to the tenant's notice. A child means a minor child living with the tenant or an adult child who is legally incapacitated. The statute says the documentation requirement is satisfied by any one of these documents, so do not ask for more or different proof, and you may not reveal the documents or the forwarding address to the person the tenant identified as the source of danger (`edu-dv-confidentiality-mi`). In federally assisted housing a separate federal list applies to the federal protections: there you may ask in writing for documentation, the tenant has 14 business days to provide it (if documents conflict, you may require third-party documentation within 30 calendar days), and the tenant chooses among a HUD certification form, a statement signed by a victim service provider, attorney, or medical or mental health professional, a police, court or agency record, or at your discretion the tenant's own statement.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText:
Michigan's Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act gives tenants and applicants with a disability two housing rights, and no lease term can take them away.

(1) Accommodations: you may not refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy residential property, for example an exception to a parking, pet or payment-method rule; the Act's general duty is to accommodate a person with a disability in housing unless you show the accommodation would impose an undue hardship.

(2) Modifications: you may not refuse to let a person with a disability make reasonable modifications of the premises the person occupies or will occupy, at that person's expense, when they may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises (grab bars, a ramp, lever handles). In a rental you may, if reasonable, make your permission depend on the renter's agreement to restore the interior to its earlier condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted; an optional clause does this (`disability-modification-restoration-mn`). Michigan does not require the lease to state that condition, and has no rule of its own on a restoration escrow.

Federal rules for dwellings the Fair Housing Act covers bar raising the customary security deposit for a person with a disability, but where needed to make sure restoration can be paid for they let you negotiate, as part of the restoration agreement, payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account, not more than the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant; they also let you ask for a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with any required permits.

In Michigan, money you hold that is returnable when the unit comes back in the required condition is a security deposit, so the cautious course is to hold any restoration escrow under the deposit act and keep it, with any other deposit, within the cap of 1 1/2 months' rent.

A disability, for housing, is a physical or mental characteristic that substantially limits one or more major life activities and is unrelated to the person's ability to acquire, rent or maintain property, including a history of one or being regarded as having one; the rights belong to a person with a disability who lives or will live in the unit.

The Act's exemption for an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer and for renting rooms in a home where you or your immediate family live covers its discrimination section, not the accommodation and modification section, so in Michigan those duties apply even to small owner-occupied buildings that the federal Fair Housing Act's exemptions might leave out.

New buildings of 4 or more units with an elevator, and ground-floor units in other buildings of 4 or more units, first occupied after March 13, 1991, must also meet accessible-design rules. A person may sue for injunctive relief and damages, including reasonable attorney fees. Federal law (the Fair Housing Act) sets the same two duties for covered dwellings.

title: Penalties for Refusing a Service Animal
bodyText: Michigan has no criminal penalty for refusing an assistance animal in a rental home (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). A refusal can still be unlawful: refusing a reasonable accommodation, such as an exception to a no-pets rule for a person with a disability, violates the Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act, and the remedy is a civil suit for injunctive relief and damages, including reasonable attorney fees (`edu-disability-accommodation-mi`, `edu-assistance-animals-mi`). The criminal rule Michigan has is for a public accommodation. It must change its policies to permit a service animal (a dog, or a miniature horse, individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability); where the animal's service isn't obvious, staff may ask only whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it has been trained to perform, and may not require documentation or ask about the disability; it may not isolate the person, treat the person less favorably, or charge a fee or surcharge it doesn't charge others; and it may ask that the animal be removed only if it is out of control and the handler doesn't take effective action, or it is not housebroken. Violating those rules is a misdemeanor. Whether this law reaches a rental property depends on the federal Americans with Disabilities Act definition of a public accommodation, which the Michigan statute adopts. That definition covers places of lodging (an inn, hotel or motel, or a facility renting rooms for stays that are mainly 30 days or less with hotel-like services) and sales or rental and other service establishments; it does not list apartments or rented homes. So the homes themselves are generally outside it, while a leasing office open to the public may be a rental or service establishment. The cautious course is to treat a leasing office or any other area you open to the public as covered, and to handle animals in the homes themselves under the fair housing accommodation rules. Separately, anyone who willfully and maliciously harasses, injures or interferes with a service animal commits a misdemeanor, and falsely claiming to have a service animal in a public place is a misdemeanor; neither sets a housing documentation procedure.

title: Questions and Forms About Protected Traits
bodyText: Michigan's civil rights acts reach the questions and forms, not only the decision. A person engaging in a real estate transaction, which includes renting, may not use an application form, or make a record of inquiry in connection with a prospective rental, that indicates directly or indirectly an intent to make a preference, limitation, specification or discrimination based on religion, race, color, national origin, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, familial status or marital status (Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act) or disability (Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act); the same goes for statements, advertisements, notices and signs. You may require applicants to supply information about their financial, business or employment status, or other information designed solely to determine creditworthiness, but not information about disabilities for reasons contrary to the disability act. Information about marital status may be obtained when necessary to prepare a deed or other instrument of conveyance. You may require an applicant's Social Security number to obtain a background check for a rental. If you, with related entities, are a landlord of 5 or more rental units, you also may not publish or display a communication indicating a preference, limitation or requirement based on source of income (`edu-source-of-income-mi`). Michigan's owner-occupant exemptions (a building of 2 units or fewer where you or an immediate family member lives in one, rooms in a home where you or your immediate family live, and, under the civil rights act only, renting your own home for up to 12 months where you lived in it as your home for at least 3 months immediately before the tenant moves in and it remains your legal residence) lift these Michigan rules, but the federal Fair Housing Act's ban on discriminatory notices, statements and advertisements reaches every owner, including small owners otherwise outside federal law. Where the federal Fair Housing Act applies, HUD's rule also bars asking whether an applicant, a household member or an associate has a disability, or about its nature or severity, except questions asked of all applicants about the ability to meet the requirements of tenancy, eligibility for housing or a priority limited to people with disabilities, current illegal drug use, and convictions for illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. A safe practice: ask every applicant the same written questions, limited to what your written screening criteria need (`edu-tenant-screening-mi`, `edu-fair-housing-mi`).

title: Children and Familial Status
bodyText: Michigan does not require a lease to say anything about children (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched), but it bars treating households with children differently. Under the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act you may not refuse to rent, set different terms, conditions or privileges, misrepresent availability, or advertise or ask questions indicating a preference because of familial status: one or more individuals under 18 living with a parent or other person having custody or in the process of securing custody, or with that person's designee with written permission; a pregnant individual counts as a parent. A lease or other instrument that limits use or occupancy because of familial status is void, except within the senior-housing exemption, and a lease term that discriminates is barred (`edu-truth-in-renting-mi`).
