Exemptions: a building of 2 units or fewer where the owner or an immediate family member lives in one, renting rooms in a home where you or your immediate family live, your own home rented for up to 12 months where you lived in it as your home for at least 3 months immediately before the tenant moved in and it remains your legal residence, and, for the familial-status and age rules only, housing that meets federal, state or local senior-citizen program requirements or is bona fide housing for persons 50 or older. That Michigan senior exemption is broader than the federal one (housing for persons 62 or older, or 55-or-older housing where at least 80 percent of occupied units have a resident 55 or older and the community publishes and follows age policies), so a 50-or-older community must also qualify under federal law to refuse families with children; housing financed by the Michigan State Housing Development Authority uses a 55-or-older test. Occupancy limits: no Michigan statute sets persons per bedroom, and a limit that has the effect of excluding families with children can be challenged; the Housing Law's air-space minimums apply where that law applies (`edu-occupancy-standard-mi`). Children born or arriving during a tenancy: no Michigan rule speaks to apartments or houses, so the familial-status ban applies as for any applicant. Mobile home parks have their own rule: a park rule that bars children who were approved under earlier rules may not be enforced against a resident unless it was in force before the resident was approved, and a new rule barring children or more children can't be enforced against existing residents until 1 year after notice to them. This timing rule does not make a children ban lawful: outside housing for older persons, a park rule barring children is itself barred by the familial-status rules. These are Michigan's exemptions; federal fair housing law has its own (`edu-portfolio-thresholds-mi`).

title: Size Thresholds in Michigan Rental Law
bodyText: Michigan's core landlord-tenant laws (deposits, the Truth in Renting Act, repair covenants, summary proceedings) apply to every residential landlord whatever the number of units you own; there is no general small-landlord exemption. A few rules turn on size, and each exemption with several conditions requires all of them. (1) Source of income: the ban on refusing or treating tenants differently because of a voucher or other lawful source of income does not apply if you, together with every related entity (anyone who controls you, is controlled by you or is under common control with you), are a landlord of fewer than 5 rental units in Michigan; count all units across your entities (`edu-source-of-income-mi`). (2) Owner-occupied buildings: the civil rights and disability acts' discrimination bans do not apply to renting a unit in a building of not more than 2 units if the owner or an immediate family member (spouse, parent, child or sibling) lives in one of them, or to renting rooms in a single-family home where you or your immediate family live; both conditions are needed, and the disability act's accommodation and modification duties still apply (`edu-disability-accommodation-mi`). (3) Your own home: renting your home for not more than 12 months is exempt from the civil rights act's housing bans only if you occupied and maintained it as your home for at least 3 months immediately before the tenant moved in and it remains your legal residence. (4) Accessible design: disability design rules apply to buildings of 4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991 (ground-floor units, or every unit if the building has an elevator). (5) Housing Law building size: where the Housing Law applies, a multiple dwelling housing more than 8 families in which the owner does not live must have a responsible person designated by the owner (`edu-housing-law-mi`). (6) Federal Fair Housing Act: a private owner of not more than 3 single-family houses who rents without a broker or agent and without a discriminatory advertisement is outside most of the federal act, and so is an owner-occupant of a building of up to 4 units; but anyone who owns a dwelling for 5 or more families, or made 3 or more rentals as principal in the past 12 months, is in the business of renting and gets no single-family exemption, and the federal advertising ban applies to everyone. These Michigan and federal tests differ, so an owner can be exempt under one and covered by the other. Some rules turn on place, not portfolio: the Housing Law of Michigan applies only in cities, villages and townships of 10,000 or more, and to single-family and 2-family homes only in places of 100,000 or more unless the local body adopts it (`edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-scope-mi`). For property-tax appeals, real property with fewer than 4 rental units counts as residential property in the Tax Tribunal's residential property and small claims division.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant or applicant that a registered sex offender lives in or near the property, to check the registry, or to put a registry notice in an ordinary lease.

The Michigan State Police keep a public internet website showing, for each registered individual, the name, address and other information the Sex Offenders Registration Act lists, and local police posts, law enforcement agencies and sheriff's departments make that information available for public inspection; you may pass on information from the public website, while divulging nonpublic registration information is a misdemeanor with a civil action for treble damages.

One case is different: if you lease a home of 1 to 4 units with an option to purchase, the Seller Disclosure Act applies, and its statutory disclosure statement (delivered to the tenant-buyer, with compliance noted on the lease, an addendum or a separate document) advises that sex offender registry information is available to the public.

You may add an optional lease notice pointing tenants to the public registry (`sex-offender-registry-notice-mi`).

No Michigan statute bars you from renting to a registered offender or makes you enforce where one lives; a court must order certain probationers convicted of a listed offense not to reside within 1,000 feet of school property, a condition that binds the probationer, not you.

title: Protecting Tenant Information
bodyText: No Michigan statute generally bars a landlord from sharing a tenant's or applicant's information or sets a consent rule for doing so (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Specific rules apply. (1) Domestic violence release: you may reveal the forwarding address a tenant gives you when seeking a release only as reasonably necessary for your regular and ordinary business, and you may never intentionally reveal that address or the tenant's documents to the person the tenant named as the source of danger (`edu-dv-confidentiality-mi`). (2) Social Security numbers: if you obtain them in the ordinary course of business, you may not publicly display more than 4 sequential digits, use them as an account number, print them on a card, send them in a way visible from outside an envelope, or require them to be sent over the internet without a secure connection or encryption; a violation made with knowledge that it breaks the act is a misdemeanor; the individual may sue for actual damages for any violation, and for a knowing violation for actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees, after a written demand at least 60 days before suing. You must also have a written privacy policy for the numbers you hold (limiting access, barring unlawful disclosure, describing proper disposal), unless you hold them in compliance with the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act. (3) Data security: anyone who keeps a database with personal information (a name with a Social Security number, driver license or state ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code) must destroy that data, by shredding, erasing or otherwise making it unreadable, when it is removed from the database and not kept for another lawful purpose, and must notify affected Michigan residents without unreasonable delay after a security breach likely to cause substantial loss, injury or identity theft. Federal law also requires reasonable measures to protect consumer-report information when you dispose of it. (4) Condominium units: an owner who rents a unit must give the association a copy of the lease (or, with no written lease, the tenants' names and address, the rent and the term). (5) Address confidentiality program: a victim certified under the state program can ask government offices, employers and schools to use a substitute address; a private landlord is not on that list, but treat a participant's real address with the same care. In federally assisted housing, information a tenant gives you about domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking must be kept in strict confidence. Disclosing a tenant's information in a way that is unfair or deceptive can also raise Consumer Protection Act issues (`edu-consumer-protection-mi`).

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a residential landlord to keep a rent ledger, give a payment history, include one in a demand for possession, or produce a tenant's records on request (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched), and none requires rent receipts (`edu-no-rent-receipt-rule-mi`). But a demand for possession for nonpayment must state the amount due at the time of the demand, and the eviction complaint must show the rental period and rate, the amount due and unpaid, and the date or dates each payment became due, so keep a ledger with due dates. The records Michigan does require are specific: the deposit notice at the start of the tenancy (`security-deposit-notice-mi`), the move-in and move-out inventory checklists (`edu-condition-inspection-mi`), and the itemized notice of damages within 30 days after the tenancy ends (`security-deposit-return-mi`). In an eviction for nonpayment you must prove what is owed, so a ledger is the practical way to do it. Michigan's data laws reach landlords who hold applicants' and tenants' personal information: anyone who keeps a database with a name linked to a Social Security number, driver license or state ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code must destroy that data, by shredding, erasing or otherwise making it unreadable, when it is removed from the database and not kept for another lawful purpose, and must give affected Michigan residents notice without unreasonable delay after a security breach likely to cause substantial loss, injury or identity theft. If you obtain Social Security numbers in the ordinary course of business, you need a written privacy policy for them unless you hold them in compliance with the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, and you may not display, mail or transmit them in the ways the Social Security Number Privacy Act forbids (`edu-tenant-confidential-information-mi`). Federal law requires reasonable measures to protect consumer-report information when you dispose of it, for example shredding paper and erasing electronic media.

title: Screening Property Management Staff
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a landlord to run background checks on apartment or rental-property employees, such as managers, leasing agents or maintenance staff who hold keys, or bars hiring anyone with a particular record for that work (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The state screens one group through licensing: a person who, for a fee, leases or rents real estate for others, or engages in property management as a whole or partial vocation, must be licensed under the real estate article of the Occupational Code, and a licensed broker owes clients duties such as timely accounting for money received and confidentiality. An owner or lessor acting for its own property is exempt from that license unless it does so as a principal vocation not through a licensed broker. Hiring your own staff is otherwise ordinary employment, subject to the civil rights acts' employment rules and, if you use a consumer report to screen an employee, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act. Checking staff who will hold keys to tenants' homes is a prudent practice, not a legal duty.

title: No Work Cards for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires staff of a 55-or-older, 50-or-older or other senior housing community to hold a work card or permit, or requires the landlord to screen them (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan's work permits are for employing minors under the youth employment law, and they apply to any employer, senior housing included. What Michigan law says about senior housing for landlords is the fair housing exemption: housing that meets federal, state or local senior-citizen program requirements, or is bona fide housing for persons 50 or older, may limit occupancy by age and familial status (`edu-children-occupancy-mi`); federal law sets its own test for housing for older persons. Any tenant who has occupied a rental unit for more than 13 months and becomes eligible during the lease term to take possession of a subsidized unit in senior citizen housing (housing for people 62 or older subsidized under a government program) may end the lease on 60 days' written notice with written proof of eligibility, and every lease must say so (`early-termination-senior-infirmity-mi`). Anyone who manages property for others for a fee must be licensed as a real estate broker, or work under one as a licensed salesperson (`edu-no-employee-screening-rule-mi`).

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No Michigan statute gives a landlord a tax credit, grant or other incentive for renting to a veteran or servicemember, requires a rent preference for them, or makes veteran or military status a protected class in housing (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Two Michigan rules touch veterans who rent. Veterans' benefits are a protected source of income, so a landlord with 5 or more rental units (with related entities) may not refuse or treat a tenant differently because the rent is paid from them (`edu-source-of-income-mi`). And an eligible veteran or serviceperson who rents a homestead may claim the state homestead property tax credit on a share of the rent paid; that is the tenant's credit, not yours, though a tenant may ask you for rent information to claim it. You may offer your own concession to veterans or servicemembers if you apply it consistently and it does not work as a preference or limitation based on a protected trait such as disability, age or familial status; the library offers rent concessions only as an equal reduction in every month. Federal servicemember protections (lease termination on military orders) are covered in `edu-no-servicemember-statute-mi`.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: No Michigan statute gives a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items on a door, doorframe or elsewhere at a rental, or limits a landlord's rules on such displays (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The only display statute is for condominiums: a developer or association of co-owners may not prohibit a co-owner from displaying a single United States flag no larger than 3 by 5 feet on the exterior of the co-owner's unit; it protects owners, not their tenants, and binds associations, not landlords (`edu-no-display-rights-rule-mi`). Display rules are therefore a matter for your lease and rules (`rules-mi`), with one limit: religion is a protected class under the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, so a rule that singles out religious items, or is enforced against one faith and not others, can be discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental. Apply any rule on door and exterior decorations evenly to all displays, religious or not.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Michigan has no statute that gives tenants an affirmative right to form a tenant association or bars a landlord from interfering with one (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched), but it protects organizing through the eviction law. In summary proceedings a court may not enter a judgment for possession if the termination was intended primarily as retribution for a lawful act arising out of the tenancy, including membership in a tenant organization and a lawful activity of a tenant organization arising out of the tenancy, or if you tried to increase the tenant's obligations as a penalty for that activity and the tenant's failure to meet them was the main reason for the termination. If within 90 days before you filed the tenant sought official action against you through a court or government agency that has not been dismissed or denied, retaliation is presumed unless you prove otherwise (`edu-retaliation-mi`). Housing run by a local housing commission must have a tenant of public or subsidized housing on the commission. Mobile home parks are governed by the Mobile Home Commission Act and its rules, which this library has not read for this topic. In practice: don't raise rent, cut services, refuse renewal or start an eviction because a tenant joined or organized a tenant group, and keep a record of the independent reason for any action you take against an active member.

title: Guests and Visitors
bodyText:
No Michigan statute gives a tenant a right to receive guests, caregivers or suppliers, bars a guest fee, or limits a landlord's guest rules, so guest terms are a matter for the lease (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`).

Three Michigan rules shape them. Any guest charge must be in the lease when it is signed, since during the term you may not change lease provisions without the tenant's written consent, except for the three kinds of adjustment the Truth in Renting Act lets a lease provide for on at least 30 days' written notice; the one for rules covers only a change in rules required to protect the physical health, safety or peaceful enjoyment of tenants and guests.

Guest rules must be applied the same way to everyone and may not turn on the race, religion, sex, familial status or other protected trait of the tenant or anyone living with the tenant, and a reasonable accommodation may be needed for a live-in aide or caregiver of a tenant with a disability.

Michigan's crime of occupying a single-family or 2-family dwelling without the owner's consent for agreed consideration does not apply to a guest or family member of the owner or of a tenant, so removing an overstaying guest of a tenant runs through the lease and, if needed, the courts.

title: Political Signs, Canvassing and Candidate Access
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a landlord to let candidates, canvassers or petition circulators into an apartment building or onto rental property, or gives a tenant a right to post political or campaign signs (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Rules on canvassing, soliciting and signs are a matter for your lease and rules (`rules-mi`), applied evenly; they must not treat tenants differently because of religion, race or another trait the civil rights acts protect (`edu-fair-housing-mi`). Condominium associations and developers may not bar a co-owner from flying one United States flag, but that rule protects owners, not tenants (`edu-no-display-rights-rule-mi`). Mobile home parks are governed by the Mobile Home Commission Act and its rules, which this library has not read for this topic; check them before applying an apartment rule to a park. Local ordinances may regulate signs and door-to-door activity.

title: Reporting Duties and Police Cooperation
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a landlord, as a landlord, to cooperate with police, give them keys or access to a tenant's home, report tenants' crimes, or join a crime-free housing program (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Several duties bind any person, so they bind you and your staff when you learn something on the job. (1) Deaths: anyone who has first knowledge that a person died suddenly, unexpectedly, accidentally, violently or under suspicious circumstances, or without medical attendance in the preceding 48 hours (unless a physician can determine the cause), must immediately notify the county medical examiner; this is the usual case when a tenant is found dead in a unit (`edu-tenant-death-mi`). (2) Social gatherings: an owner, tenant or other person having control over a residence may not knowingly allow anyone under 21 to drink or possess alcohol, or anyone to use or possess a controlled substance, at a social gathering there; failing to take corrective action, which can include promptly reporting it to the police, can count as allowing it (a misdemeanor); the rule does not reach a lawful prescription or a minor's drinking for religious purposes. (3) Abuse: Michigan's child-abuse and vulnerable-adult reporting duties bind listed professions (health, education, social services, clergy, law enforcement and the like), not landlords as such, but any person who has reasonable cause to suspect child abuse or neglect may report it. Some landlord remedies depend on the police: the 24-hour notice to quit for drug activity under a lease clause requires a formal police report (`criminal-activity-mi`), and the 7-day notice for causing or threatening physical injury to someone on property you own or operate requires that the police were notified, and is not available where the person hurt or threatened is the tenant or a household member or where using it would violate federal housing regulations (`edu-dv-eviction-protection-mi`). A personal protection order is enforced by the police, and a writ of restitution after an eviction judgment by a court officer, bailiff, sheriff or local law enforcement officer the court commands, never by you. Michigan has no statute protecting a tenant's calls for police help (`edu-no-emergency-assistance-rule-mi`).

title: Drug-Free Housing Terms in Michigan
bodyText:
Michigan does not require a drug-free housing addendum, but its eviction law rewards one. If a lease clause provides for termination because a tenant, a member of the tenant's household or another person under the tenant's control unlawfully manufactured, delivered, possessed with intent to deliver, or possessed a controlled substance (schedule 1, 2 or 3) on the leased premises, and a formal police report has been filed alleging it, you may give a 24-hour notice to quit or demand for possession instead of the usual notice; without such a clause that route is unavailable.

The library's Michigan clause provides it (`criminal-activity-mi`), so Michigan uses that clause rather than a separate addendum.

The shared drug-free housing addenda written for other states are not used in Michigan, because Michigan's recreational marihuana law lets you prohibit or regulate marihuana on your property but says a lease may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing marihuana or consuming it by means other than smoking; an addendum that bans all marihuana use or possession in the home would be unenforceable to that extent (`smoking-policy-mi`).

Separately, an owner, tenant or other person having control over a residence may not knowingly allow anyone to use or possess a controlled substance at a social gathering there.

In Housing Choice Voucher and public housing, federal rules require the lease to make drug-related criminal activity by a tenant, household member or guest a ground for ending the tenancy, and the HUD addendum supplies that language; federal law also protects a tenant who is the victim of abuse-related crime.

title: No Lease Translation Duty in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires you to translate a lease or rental notice, to give a tenant the lease in the language you advertised or negotiated in, or to provide a translation when a tenant has limited English, and none says which version controls if you sign a lease in two languages (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan's prescribed lease text is in English: the Truth in Renting Act notice and the domestic violence rights statement must appear in the words the statutes give (`truth-in-renting-notice-mi`, `dv-release-notice-mi`), and the Truth in Renting notice has its own minimum type size. Michigan's language-access law binds state departments and agencies providing public services, not landlords. If you advertise or negotiate in another language, offering a translated copy is good practice, and making clear which version controls avoids disputes; but the Consumer Protection Act makes it an unlawful practice to take advantage of a tenant's inability to understand the language of an agreement you present when you know or reasonably should know of it, and gross discrepancies between what you say orally and the written lease are also unlawful (`edu-consumer-protection-mi`); with a tenant of limited English, explain the lease in a language the tenant understands or offer a translation. Treating applicants differently because of national origin, including through language rules that work as a proxy for it, can violate the civil rights acts (`edu-fair-housing-mi`).

title: Student Housing in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan has no special landlord-tenant rule for student housing: no exemption from the deposit act, the Truth in Renting Act, the repair covenants or summary proceedings for renting to students, and no separate duties for privately owned student buildings (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Student status is not a protected class, and the civil rights acts have no student exemption, so the usual fair housing rules apply (`edu-fair-housing-mi`). Michigan's student-housing statutes are about schools: public universities' and colleges' powers to build and finance dormitories, and Fire Prevention Code drill rules. A college or university must hold fire drills (one each in the fall and spring semesters, and in summer if occupied) and keep exits unobstructed in its dormitories: on-campus buildings it owns, leases, manages or controls that house more than 16 unrelated people without individual cooking facilities. If you lease a building to a college for that use, agree in writing who runs the drills; an ordinary off-campus apartment building leased to students is not such a dormitory. Parental guarantees, joint liability among roommates and early termination at the end of a semester are matters for your lease (`joint-liability`); the deposit act's notices and deadlines apply to each tenancy (`security-deposit-return-mi`). Local ordinances in college towns may add rules.

title: When Illegal Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: Two Michigan statutes tie a lease to how the premises are used. (1) Prostitution and gambling: if the tenant of a dwelling house is convicted of, or is guilty of, keeping a house of ill-fame or a common gaming house there, the lease becomes void at your option, and you then have the same remedy to recover possession as against a tenant holding over after the term ends (summary proceedings, `edu-eviction-process-mi`). The same law makes it a misdemeanor for anyone to let a dwelling knowing the tenant intends to use it as a house of ill-fame or for prostitution or gambling, to knowingly permit that use, or to receive rent for a dwelling, room or apartment used that way with reasonable cause to believe it. (2) Nuisance abatement: a building or place used for prostitution, gambling, lewdness, illegal drug manufacture or sale, illegal liquor sales, animal fighting, human trafficking or armed violence is a public nuisance; the owner or person who leases or maintains it is guilty of a nuisance, and the attorney general, the prosecutor, a local government attorney or any county resident can sue to abate it. On judgment the court may order the contents removed and sold and the building closed for up to 1 year, and knowledge of the nuisance need not be proven. An owner can get the building back by paying the costs and posting a bond of $1,000 to $50,000 to abate the nuisance. For drug activity, a lease clause also gives you a 24-hour notice route (`criminal-activity-mi`, `edu-drug-free-housing-addendum-mi`). Housing run by a local housing commission may end a tenancy only for just cause, which includes use of the unit for an unlawful purpose. Michigan's library uses its own use and criminal-activity clauses (`residential-use-only`, `criminal-activity-mi`) rather than another state's purpose-limitation clause.

title: Landlord Registration and Licensing
bodyText: Michigan has no statewide landlord or rental registration and no state rental license. Two state rules touch registration. (1) The Housing Law of Michigan applies only in cities, villages and townships of 10,000 or more people, and to single-family and 2-family homes only in places of 100,000 or more unless the local governing body adopts it (`edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-scope-mi`). Where it applies, the local enforcing agency may keep a registry of owners and premises. If it does, the owner of a multiple dwelling or rooming house with units offered for rent for more than 6 months of a calendar year must register the owner's name, the address of the owner's residence or usual place of business and the location of the building within 60 days after any part of it is offered for occupancy, and must add the name and place of business of any agent who manages it. You apply for the Housing Law certificate of compliance when you register, and units in a multiple dwelling or rooming house may not be occupied until one is issued; if you do not register, any occupant may apply (`edu-certificate-of-occupancy-mi`). (2) In a city with an administrative hearings bureau for blight violations, the city may not issue you a blight violation notice during an inspection of a residential rental unless you first get a written correction notice and a reasonable chance to correct, or the violation is a direct result of your action or inaction and creates an emergency (for example a flooded basement or no heat). That protection covers registered landlords in a city whose rental inspection program requires registration, and every landlord in a city without one. No Michigan statute bars a local government from requiring rental registration, licensing or inspection; the state ban on local rent control reaches only the amount of rent (`edu-rent-control-mi`). Detroit, Grand Rapids, Ann Arbor, Lansing and other cities run their own registration and inspection programs. Michigan has no rule that an out-of-state owner must hire an in-state broker or keep an in-state contact (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). If someone else manages your rentals for pay, leasing or renting another's property for a fee is property management, which is part of the definition of a real estate broker, and no one may practice a licensed occupation without the license; an owner renting its own property is exempt unless it does so as a principal vocation not through a licensed broker.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Michigan has no lease registry, and no Michigan statute requires you to record or register a residential lease or makes a tenant's rights depend on recording (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Recording matters only for a lease longer than 3 years. Michigan's recording act covers every written instrument that creates an interest in real estate, except, among others, a lease for a term not exceeding 3 years, and an unrecorded instrument it covers is void against a later buyer who buys in good faith and for value and records first. So a lease of 3 years or less is outside that rule, while a tenant under an unrecorded longer lease risks losing it to such a buyer. The recording formalities themselves (what the register of deeds will accept) are not restated here. Whether a tenant's possession alone puts a buyer or lender on notice of the lease is a question of case law. Michigan's marketable record title act does not cut off a landlord's right to possession when a lease ends or a tenant's rights under a lease. Separately, a lease for more than 1 year must be in writing (`edu-statute-of-frauds-mi`).

title: No Good-Cause Notice Rule
bodyText: Michigan has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law for privately owned houses and apartments, so there is no notice telling a tenant whether such a law covers the unit and nothing of that kind to put in the lease (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). A fixed term ends on its end date, and a month-to-month or other tenancy at will ends on 1 month's notice from either party (where rent is payable at intervals of less than 3 months, notice equal to the interval between payments is enough), without a reason (`edu-termination-notice-mi`, `edu-for-cause-eviction-mi`). Five limits apply. (1) Retaliation: a court will not enter a judgment for possession if the termination was intended primarily as a penalty for the tenant's attempt to enforce rights or for a complaint to a government authority about a health or safety code violation; a complaint by official action within 90 days before the eviction case raises a presumption of retaliation (`edu-retaliation-mi`). (2) If you receive Michigan State Housing Development Authority assistance for multifamily housing under the authority's housing assistance chapter, you must agree in writing not to evict a tenant without just cause, as the public housing law defines it (a lease or rules violation, unlawful use of the unit, or keeping an unsafe, unsanitary or unhealthful condition); check your assistance documents. (3) If your tenant has a federal Housing Choice Voucher, during the lease term you may end the tenancy only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law tied to the occupancy or use of the premises, or other good cause; during the initial term, other good cause must be something the family did or failed to do, so it cannot be your wish to live in the unit, sell or renovate it, or charge more. You must give the tenant a written notice stating the grounds, at or before the start of the eviction case, and give the housing agency a copy of any eviction notice. (4) Housing run by a local government unit and mobile home park lots carry their own just-cause rules; mobile home parks are outside this library. (5) If your building has HUD project-based rental subsidy, federal rules govern ending the tenancy: the written termination notice must state specific reasons and be served by first-class mail and by delivery at the unit, and the federal rules set when it may be given and take effect; federal good-cause rules for those programs and for low-income housing tax credit properties are not restated here.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a state agency to publish a guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, requires you to give a tenant such a guide before signing or at renewal, or requires a signed acknowledgment of one (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). What Michigan requires is in the lease itself: the Truth in Renting notice, printed in a prominent place in at least 12-point type, telling the tenant that Michigan law establishes rights and obligations for parties to rental agreements, and the name and address at which notices to you are to be given (`truth-in-renting-notice-mi`, `edu-truth-in-renting-statements-mi`). If you take a security deposit, you also give the tenant the deposit notice and the inventory checklists (`security-deposit-notice-mi`, `edu-condition-inspection-mi`). The state health department must make lead-poisoning educational materials for owners and tenants of residential dwellings available on request, but that puts no duty on you to hand them to a tenant (`edu-no-lead-state-notices-mi`).

title: Tenant Rights Statement: the Truth in Renting Notice
bodyText: Michigan has no state-agency statement or summary of tenant rights that you must attach to the lease, put on its first page, have each tenant sign or acknowledge, or give before you may sue (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Its rights statement is the Truth in Renting notice, which the lease itself must carry: every written rental agreement for residential premises must state, in a prominent place in type at least 12-point (or legible print with letters at least 1/8 inch), a notice substantially in the statutory form telling the tenant that Michigan law establishes rights and obligations for parties to rental agreements, that the agreement must comply with the Truth in Renting Act, and that the tenant may want a lawyer's help with questions. The lease must also state the name and address at which notices to you are to be given. The library supplies both (`truth-in-renting-notice-mi`, `lessor-notice-address-mi`). If a lease leaves either out and you do not cure within 20 days after a tenant's written notice, the tenant may sue to void the lease, for an injunction, and for $500 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus court costs and statutory attorney fees; no prior notice is needed if you actually knew the statement was missing when the lease was signed (how to cure: `edu-truth-in-renting-statements-mi`). The act does not cover temporary hotel, motel or tourist stays or an owner's principal residence rented occasionally during a temporary absence (`edu-scope-mi`).

title: Renting Houses: Zoning and Investor Limits
bodyText: No Michigan statute limits renting a house in a single-family zone, makes renting depend on the owner living on the lot, or creates a state lot-split or two-unit program with an owner-occupancy or rental-term condition (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Zoning is local, and some Michigan communities limit rentals by ordinance; the state ban on local rent control covers only rent amounts (`edu-rent-control-mi`). Two state rules bear on owning or renting a house. (1) From July 21, 2026, a large institutional investor may not buy, or contract to buy, a single-family home in Michigan (a structure with 2 or fewer dwelling units, each for one household, not a manufactured home). A large institutional investor is a for-profit entity in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing or holding single-family homes that, alone or with others, controls more than 100 single-family homes in Michigan and manages or has a net value of $375,000,000 or more. Exceptions include build-to-rent purchases of new homes, qualifying renovate-to-rent purchases, listed homeownership programs, acquisitions by a lender or servicer after a default, reorganizations of homes owned before that date and certain state-approved housing for income-qualified households. A violation carries a civil fine of up to $25,000 per home. The rule limits buying, not renting homes already owned. (2) A condominium association may restrict rentals through its condominium documents; an amendment does not affect a written lease that complies with the law and was signed before the amendment took effect (`edu-condominium-leasing-mi`). Separately, the zoning act makes a family child care home a permitted residential use in county and township residential zones, and requires zoning ordinances to let an occupant of a single-family residence teach a craft or fine art there (`edu-family-child-care-mi`, `edu-home-business-mi`).

title: Local Health Department Rules and Orders
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires you to give a tenant the local health department's housing or rental rules on request, or to refer a tenant to the health department (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Local health rules reach you directly, though. Your repair covenant includes complying with the applicable health and safety laws of the state and of the local unit of government where the premises are located, except where the violation was caused by the tenant's wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct (`edu-habitability-mi`). A local health department may order an owner to avoid, correct or remove, at the owner's expense, a building or condition that violates health laws or that the health officer reasonably believes is a nuisance, unsanitary condition or cause of illness; if the order is not obeyed, the department may have the work done and the owner pays, unpaid costs are assessed against the property and collected like taxes, and an occupant who caused or permitted the condition is liable to the owner for that amount. When a local health officer finds an imminent danger to health or life, the officer must inform the people affected and order immediate action, which can include keeping people out of the danger area. Where the Housing Law applies, a city or village or its board of health may set housing standards stricter than the Housing Law's minimums (`edu-housing-law-mi`). A tenant's complaint to a government authority about a health or safety code violation is protected from retaliatory eviction (`edu-retaliation-mi`). Local health department and city housing rules are not in this library.

title: Lead Safe Housing Registry
bodyText: Michigan has no lead-safe certificate that you must obtain before renting or attach to a lease (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). It has a lead safe housing registry, which the state health department keeps and publishes on its website. If you own target housing that you offer for rent or lease as a residence, and it has been abated of lead-based paint hazards or has had interim controls performed to control them, as determined through a lead-based paint investigation by a certified risk assessor, you must register it with the department, free, on the department's form. Target housing is housing built before 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities (unless a child aged 6 or under lives or is expected to live there), a 0-bedroom dwelling, and an unoccupied unit awaiting demolition. The form gives the owner's name, the building's address and date of construction, and the date and description of each lead-based paint activity with the name of the certified worker or risk assessor who did it and its results; you must also give the department a copy of each lead-based paint report or document you must file with the federal government. Owners of other rental dwellings may register voluntarily, for a fee. Violating the state lead law or its rules can bring an administrative fine of up to $2,000 for a first violation, $5,000 for a second and $10,000 for a third or later, for each violation or each day it continues. Registration is not a lease term: the federal lead disclosure still goes with every lease of pre-1978 housing (`lead-based-paint`), and Michigan's crime of renting to a family with a lead-poisoned child despite a known hazard is in `edu-lead-hazard-mi`.

title: No State Lead Notice Beyond the Federal Disclosure
bodyText:
Michigan adds no lead notice, certificate, pamphlet or disclosure of its own that you must deliver with a lease.

The lead paperwork for a lease is federal: before a tenant is obligated under a lease of target housing (generally housing built before 1978), you must give the EPA-approved pamphlet, disclose any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards and any available records or reports, and the lease (or an attachment) must contain the federal Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure, the list of records, and the tenant's acknowledgment (`lead-based-paint`).

The federal rules exempt, among others, leases of housing found lead-based-paint free by a certified inspector, leases of 100 days or less that cannot be renewed or extended, and renewals where everything was already disclosed and nothing new has come to light.

Two Michigan lead rules sit beside the federal disclosure but are not lease notices. If target housing you offer for rent has been abated or had interim controls after a certified risk assessor's investigation, you must register it on the state lead safe housing registry.

And it is a misdemeanor to rent or keep renting to a family with a minor child found to have 10 micrograms or more of lead per deciliter of venous blood when you have had actual knowledge of a lead-based paint hazard in the unit for at least 90 days and have not acted in good faith to reduce it; you are presumed to know only if you signed an acknowledgment of the hazard at a risk assessment or were served notice of it by first-class mail with a return receipt. Keep the federal disclosure with the lease.

title: Housing Code Orders and Receivership
bodyText: Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies (cities, villages and townships of 10,000 or more; single-family and 2-family homes only in places of 100,000 or more unless adopted locally: `edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-scope-mi`), code enforcement for any dwelling it regulates, not only buildings of 2 or more units, runs through violation notices, court orders and, at the end, receivership. After an inspection the enforcing agency records each violation in its registry of owners and premises and notifies you in writing of the violation, the section violated and the time to correct it; it notifies the occupant only of a serious and imminent hazard (a dangerous condition that could reasonably be expected to cause death or serious bodily harm if not corrected immediately). If such a hazard exists where the premises cannot be vacated, the agency orders it corrected in the shortest reasonable time and you must tell the agency within 3 days that you have begun. If you do not obey the order, the enforcing agency, or an owner or occupant of the premises, may sue to enforce the Housing Law. The court may order repairs, authorize the agency to repair or remove the building, let a complaining occupant who did not cause the condition correct it and deduct the cost from rent, or let you correct a condition the occupant caused and charge the cost to the occupant or the security deposit; unpaid repair or removal costs can be made a lien on the property. Once such a suit has been brought against the owner, the court may appoint a receiver (the municipality, a local agency or officer, or any competent person) to repair and rehabilitate the building into compliance, or remove it if ordered. The receiver may collect the rents and hold them against earlier assignees of the rents, manage and let units, issue receivership certificates and contract for the work, and the court may make the receiver's expenses a lien on the property. A tenant who paid rent to a receiver, into a Housing Law escrow, or under a court repair order has a defense to an eviction for nonpayment of that rent. Separately, if you let unsafe, unsanitary or unhealthful conditions that violate the Housing Law go unabated, an occupant may, after notice to you and your failure to correct, sue you for actual damages and, for a continuing interference, an injunction. Dangerous buildings may also be ordered demolished, made safe or maintained after a hearing, and cities may add their own procedures.

title: No Code Violation or Condemnation Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires you to tell a prospective or current tenant about outstanding code violations, inspection orders, or condemnation or vacate orders, or to state them in the lease (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Other rules do that work. Where the Housing Law applies (`edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-scope-mi`): units in a multiple dwelling or rooming house may not be occupied unless a certificate of compliance has been issued, and while a certificate is withheld or suspended, premises not yet occupied may not be occupied and occupied premises may be ordered vacated (`edu-certificate-of-occupancy-mi`, `edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-mi`); the enforcing agency itself notifies the occupant in writing of a serious and imminent hazard; it must make available to the public a checklist of commonly recurring violations for examining premises offered for occupancy; and when a suit to enforce the Housing Law is filed, a notice that the case is pending is filed with the county register of deeds. When police find an illegal drug manufacturing site, they post a written warning on the premises, and if the property is found likely contaminated the enforcing agency orders it vacated until the owner's decontamination certification is accepted (`edu-meth-mi`). You must keep the premises fit and in compliance with health and safety laws (`edu-habitability-mi`), and failing to reveal a material fact that tends to mislead a tenant and that the tenant could not reasonably know is an unfair practice under the Consumer Protection Act, which reaches leases (`edu-consumer-protection-mi`). Resolve any order before you rent, and tell an applicant about any condition you know of that affects the unit. Cities may require more.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty; Inventory Checklists
bodyText: Michigan has no separate notice telling a tenant about a right to a move-in or move-out inspection, and no penalty tied to such a notice (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Its rule is the inventory checklist. If you require a security deposit, you must use inventory checklists at the start and end of the occupancy: give the tenant 2 blank copies of the commencement checklist, carrying at the top of the first page, in 12-point boldface type, the statutory notice that the tenant should complete it and return it within 7 days after obtaining possession and may request a copy of the last termination inventory checklist; and at the end complete a termination checklist listing all damages you claim the tenant caused (`edu-condition-inspection-mi`). The deposit act names no penalty for skipping the checklists themselves, and whether a court would refuse deductions you cannot support with them is a question of case law, so use both checklists every time. The penalties Michigan does set are on the return process: your notice of damages may not include damage claimed on a previous tenant's termination checklist, if you do not mail an itemized notice of damages within 30 days after the tenancy ends, you are treated as agreeing that no damages are due and must return the full deposit immediately; and if you do not comply fully with the rules for keeping a disputed amount you waive all claimed damages and owe the tenant double the amount of the deposit retained (`edu-security-deposit-penalty-mi`). A lease term waiving the deposit rules is void (`edu-security-deposit-nonwaiver-mi`).

title: Rent Suspension Without a Certificate of Compliance
bodyText: Where the Housing Law applies (`edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-scope-mi`) and the unit is in a multiple dwelling or rooming house that needs a Housing Law certificate of compliance (`edu-certificate-of-occupancy-mi`), the tenant's duty to pay rent under the lease or any statute is suspended while the premises have no certificate of compliance or while an issued certificate is suspended. The suspended rent is paid into an escrow account set up by the enforcing agency, which pays it to you or anyone else authorized to make repairs, to cover correcting the violations. Suspension does not begin until you have had a reasonable time after notice of violations to apply for a temporary certificate, and it does not apply if you show that the occupant caused the hazardous conditions. Rent is due again under the lease once the certificate is reinstated or a temporary certificate issues. If the occupant ends the tenancy before repairs begin, the agency returns unspent escrow for the unexpired part of the rental period. If a tenant withholds rent but does not pay it into the escrow, you may sue for rent and possession, subject to the tenant's defenses; rent paid into the escrow (or to a court-appointed receiver or under a court repair order) is a defense to an eviction for nonpayment. While a certificate is withheld or suspended, the agency may order occupied premises vacated until reinspection and proof of compliance, and premises not yet occupied may not be occupied. A property found likely contaminated by illegal drug manufacturing must stay vacated until decontamination is certified and accepted (`edu-meth-mi`). Outside these rules Michigan has no general statute barring rent after a condemnation or vacate order (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched), but in an eviction case the court deducts rent excused by your breach of the lease or the repair covenants (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-mi`). If your tenant's rent comes through the state rent vendoring program and the state ends your participation because of a housing code hazard, you may not evict the tenant based solely on that; a tenant evicted in violation may recover treble damages, costs and attorney fees. Cities may add rules.

title: No Code Variance Notice Rule
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires you to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a notice of a variance, exception or waiver from a housing, health or building code that applies to the rental (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Variances exist in two state laws. Under the Housing Law, where it applies (`edu-housing-law-mi`), no local ordinance or decision may repeal, modify or dispense with its minimum requirements, except that a board of appeals' decision, where the strict letter of the law causes practical difficulties or unnecessary and unreasonable hardship, is treated as a reasonable application of the act. Under the state construction code, a board of appeals may, after a public hearing, grant a specific variance from a substantive code requirement for an exceptional, practical difficulty, on written conditions; breaching a condition automatically invalidates the variance and any permit, license and certificate granted on it. If a variance affects a rental unit, keep its conditions met and tell the tenant in writing, before signing, what it allows; failing to reveal a material fact that misleads a tenant can be an unfair practice under the Consumer Protection Act (`edu-consumer-protection-mi`). Local health and zoning variances are set locally.

title: Certificates of Occupancy and Compliance
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy or of compliance, to give the tenant a copy, or to attach one to the lease (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Two certificates matter before you rent. (1) Under the state construction code, a newly built building or structure may not be used or occupied, in whole or in part, until the enforcing agency issues a certificate of use and occupancy, and an altered one may not be used or occupied until a new certificate issues (an existing use not interrupted during the alteration may continue for 30 days after it is finished). The agency must issue it within 5 business days after a written application when the building qualifies, and may issue a temporary certificate for parts that can be occupied safely before all work is done. For a new dwelling with units for rent, the certificate of use and occupancy also serves as its first Housing Law certificate of compliance. (2) Where the Housing Law applies (`edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-scope-mi`), units in multiple dwellings and rooming houses may not be occupied unless the enforcing agency has issued a certificate of compliance, ordinarily after inspection. It will not issue one while conditions are a hazard to the health or safety of those who may occupy the premises, and it may suspend one when such conditions appear later. You apply when you register with the agency's registry (if you do not, an occupant may apply), the fee is $10 when the certificate is issued, and temporary certificates are available in listed cases. While a required certificate is missing or suspended, the tenant's rent is suspended and paid into escrow, with exceptions (`edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-mi`). Many cities run their own certificate or rental-license programs. Don't rent a unit, or part of a building, that lacks a certificate it needs.

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Michigan freezes the codes its state agencies adopt at a named edition. Under the Administrative Procedures Act, an agency that adopts a national code by reference must identify it by date, and the reference does not cover later amendments and editions; to use a newer edition the agency must amend its rule or adopt a new one. The state construction code works that way: it consists of the International Residential, Building, Mechanical, Plumbing, Existing Building and Energy Conservation Codes and the National Electrical Code, with Michigan amendments, adopted by rule, and the statute sets update cycles (at least every 3 years for most parts; for the residential code, not more often than every 3 years nor less often than every 6). The rules held by this library adopt the International Residential Code, 2015 edition, for 1- and 2-family dwellings (rule effective February 8, 2022), and the International Building Code and International Existing Building Code, 2021 editions (effective April 9, 2025); check with the state Bureau of Construction Codes for any later update. A newer national edition does not apply in Michigan until the rules adopt it. Under the residential code, the legal occupancy of a structure existing when the code was adopted may continue without change, except as that code, the International Property Maintenance Code or the International Fire Code specifically covers; new work must meet the code in force when it is permitted. A city may adopt a property maintenance, building or fire code by reference in an ordinance, which must clearly identify the code it adopts. The Housing Law's standards are written into the statute itself and are minimums that cities may exceed (`edu-housing-law-mi`). Your lease cannot freeze a standard at the signing date: the repair covenant requires you to comply with the applicable health and safety laws during the term, and it may be modified only in a lease with a current term of at least 1 year (`edu-habitability-mi`, `edu-habitability-modifiable-mi`).

title: No Single-Family Rental Disclosure
bodyText: Michigan has no disclosure that applies because the rental is a single-family home, no required statement about a house's permitted occupancy, and no rule putting any disclosure on the first page of a lease (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The type-size rules Michigan does have apply to every residential rental, house or apartment: the Truth in Renting notice, in a prominent place in type at least 12-point (`truth-in-renting-notice-mi`); the security deposit notice, given within 14 days after the tenant takes possession, whose forwarding-address statement must be in 12-point boldface type at least 4 points larger than the body of the notice or lease (`security-deposit-notice-mi`); the 12-point boldface notice at the top of the first page of the inventory checklist (`edu-condition-inspection-mi`); and the 12-point boldface statement in a notice of damages (`edu-security-deposit-penalty-mi`). The Housing Law, including its air-space limits per occupant, reaches single-family and 2-family homes only in places of 100,000 or more unless the local government adopts it (`edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-occupancy-standard-mi`); local codes may set their own occupancy limits.

title: Changing Lease Terms During a Tenancy
bodyText:
Whether the lease is for a fixed term or month to month, a Michigan lease may not let you change any of its terms after the tenancy starts without the tenant's written consent, except three kinds of change the lease itself provides for, on written notice of not less than 30 days:
- (1) changes required by federal, state or local law, rule or regulation;
- (2) changes in rules relating to the property that are required to protect the physical health, safety or peaceful enjoyment of tenants and guests; and
- (3) changes in rent to cover added operating costs from increases in ad valorem property taxes, charges for electricity, heating fuel, water or sanitary sewer services consumed at the property, or premiums for liability, fire or worker compensation insurance.

A lease term going further is void and exposes you to the Truth in Renting Act's remedies. The library offers each route as a Michigan clause: `legally-required-changes-mi` for (1), `rules-mi` for (2) and `rent-cost-adjustment-mi` for (3).

Michigan has no statute setting a notice period for changing the rent or other terms of a month-to-month tenancy, no longer notice for raising a fee the lease already provides, and no rule that a change of terms needs a full termination notice.

Outside the three routes, get the tenant's written agreement to the change, or end the periodic tenancy with the notice the law requires (1 month, or the interval between rent payments where rent is paid at intervals of less than 3 months) and offer a new lease on the new terms.

Whether a tenant who stays on after a notice of new terms has accepted them is a question of case law, so don't rely on silence.

A court will not enter possession where you tried to increase the tenant's obligations as a penalty for enforcing rights or complaining to a code agency and the tenant's failure to meet them was the main reason for the termination.

title: Ending a Lease So You or Family Can Move In
bodyText:
Michigan has no statute that gives, limits or conditions ending a tenancy so that you or a family member can move in, and no general just-cause rule.

A month-to-month or other tenancy at will may be ended for that reason, or any other lawful reason, by 1 month's notice, or notice equal to the interval between rent payments where rent is paid at intervals of less than 3 months.

A fixed-term lease runs to its end date unless the lease itself reserves an early-termination right; if it says nothing, you have no right to end it early to move in. Michigan's summary-proceedings statute lets you recover possession from a tenant who holds over after the lease is terminated under a power to terminate provided in the lease.

If you may want the home back during the term, use the optional owner-occupancy clause (`owner-occupancy-termination-ar`), which lets you end a fixed term on written notice of at least the number of days you choose (not less than 30), effective at the end of a monthly rental period, for occupancy by you or the family member named in it. Michigan sets no minimum period you must then live there and requires no relocation payment.

If the tenant does not leave, only a court can remove the tenant.

Limits: a court will not enter possession if the termination was intended primarily as a penalty for the tenant's enforcing rights or complaining to a code agency, and a complaint by official action within 90 days before the case raises a presumption of retaliation, so record when and why you decided to move in.

If your tenant has a federal Housing Choice Voucher, you may not end the tenancy during the initial lease term because you want the unit for personal or family use. If you receive Michigan State Housing Development Authority assistance for multifamily housing, you will have agreed not to evict without just cause. Fair housing law bars choosing which tenant to displace for a prohibited reason.

title: No Accessory Dwelling Unit Statute
bodyText:
No Michigan statute addresses accessory dwelling units: none requires local governments to allow them, bars an owner-occupancy requirement, sets a minimum rental term, or otherwise limits renting one. Whether you may build or rent an accessory unit, and on what conditions (owner occupancy, minimum stays, parking, permits), is set by local zoning.

If you rent one, the shared `accessory-dwelling-unit-term-co` clause records the shared areas and who lives in the main house. Once rented, an accessory unit is a rental like any other: the Truth in Renting Act, the security deposit act and the repair covenants apply.

Under the state construction code, a newly built structure may not be used or occupied until a certificate of use and occupancy is issued, and an altered one generally not until a new certificate is issued, so do not rent a converted garage, basement or new unit until the building official has issued it.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires you to let a tenant run a family child care home, voids a lease term that prohibits one, or sets conditions such as insurance or liability waivers for one.

Under the Child Care Organizations Act, a family child care home is a private home in which 1 but fewer than 7 minor children are received for care and supervision for compensation for periods of less than 24 hours a day, not counting children related to an adult member of the household; a group child care home cares for more than 6 but not more than 12. Either must be a private residence in which the licensee permanently resides, and the act regulates both.

Zoning: in a county or township, a family child care home is a residential use and a permitted use in all residential zones, with no special or conditional use permit beyond what other dwellings need, and a group child care home that meets listed standards must be issued a special use permit; in a city or village, a group child care home may be issued one. These zoning rules bind local governments, not you: your lease may permit, condition or prohibit child care in the home.

The library's `residential-use-only` clause bars any commercial purpose, which can be read to cover paid child care. If you want to allow it, use the optional `family-child-care-consent-mi` clause, which conditions the permission on any required license, compliance with zoning, codes and association rules, a cap on the number of children, and liability insurance.

Under the Truth in Renting Act, any such terms may not exculpate you from liability for your own failure to perform, or negligent performance of, a duty imposed by law.

title: Home Businesses in a Rental
bodyText:
No Michigan statute gives a tenant a right to run a business from a rental home, or makes a home business lawful unless a lease or other agreement restricts it.

Home businesses are mainly a matter of local zoning. One state zoning rule exists: a zoning ordinance must provide for an occupant of a single-family residence to use it for a home occupation giving instruction in a craft or fine art within the residence, while the local government may still regulate noise, advertising, traffic, hours of operation and similar conditions. Like the family child care rule, this binds the local government, not you: your lease may limit or bar business use, and the library's `residential-use-only` clause bars any commercial purpose.

If the home is a condominium unit, the tenant must also follow the condominium documents, which may restrict business use (`hoa-compliance-mi`).

If you want to allow a home business, use the optional `home-business-permission-mi` clause, which sets conditions (licenses and permits, association rules, insurance, no disturbance) and lets you withdraw the permission without ending the lease.

title: Condominium and Association Documents and Tenants
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires a lease of a condominium unit, or of a home in a homeowners' association, to describe the association's obligations or to give the tenant the association's documents.

For condominiums the Condominium Act binds the tenant instead: tenants and other non-owner occupants must comply with all the conditions of the condominium documents (the recorded master deed and any instrument it or the bylaws refer to that affects co-owners' rights and obligations), and every lease and rental agreement must say so (`hoa-compliance-mi`).

Before renting, you must tell the association in writing at least 10 days before presenting a lease or otherwise agreeing to give possession, give it a copy of the exact lease for its review, and later give it a copy of the signed lease; if no written lease is used, give it the occupants' names and address, the rent and its due dates, and the term. If the tenant breaches the documents, the association must notify you by certified mail and give you 15 days to investigate and correct the breach before it may sue to evict the tenant and for damages, and it may hold you and the tenant liable for damage to the general common elements; if you fall behind on assessments, it may direct the tenant to pay them out of rent.

The association must make the condominium documents available to co-owners, prospective purchasers and prospective mortgagees, not to tenants, so give your tenant copies of the documents and rules that bind the unit; the optional `association-documents-delivery-mi` clause records that you did. A tenant is not a co-owner under the act, however long the lease.

Homeowners' associations outside the Condominium Act have no Michigan leasing statute; their recorded restrictions and rules bind as those documents and contract law provide, and `hoa-compliance-mi` has the tenant agree to follow them.

title: Heat in Michigan Rentals
bodyText:
No Michigan statute sets an indoor temperature you must keep, a heating season, or a rule on when a tenant may be made to supply heat.

Heat falls under general duties instead. You covenant that the premises are fit for the use intended and that you will keep them in reasonable repair and comply with state and local health and safety laws; the parties may modify those covenants only in a lease with a current term of at least 1 year, so a shorter lease cannot make the tenant responsible for repairing the heating system.

Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies (cities, villages and townships of 10,000 or more; single-family and 2-family dwellings only in places of 100,000 or more unless the local body adopts it), the owner must keep every dwelling, including its heating, in good repair.

Causing, by action or omission, the interruption of heat that the tenant procured or that you are bound to furnish is unlawful interference with possession: the tenant may recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence, and that rule cannot be waived (a temporary interruption only as necessary to make needed repairs or an inspection, as provided by law, or one made under a court order, is not unlawful interference).

A lease may make the tenant pay for heating fuel or energy.

If the building has a boiler, the state's boiler rules require periodic certificate inspections (every 2 years for a low-pressure steam heating boiler, every 3 years for a hot water heating or supply boiler), the certificate must be posted under glass in the boiler room, and operating a boiler subject to inspection without a valid certificate is a misdemeanor; low-pressure steam boilers (15 psi or less) and hot water boilers (160 psi and 250 degrees Fahrenheit or less) in a private residence or in an apartment building with a capacity of fewer than 6 families are exempt.

Building codes adopted by reference and local ordinances (Detroit, Grand Rapids, Ann Arbor, Lansing and others) may set temperature standards.

For a federally assisted unit, HUD's national standards require a permanently installed heating source in the climate zones HUD designates and bar unvented space heaters that burn gas, oil or kerosene. The library offers an optional freeze-protection clause for homes where the tenant controls the thermostat (heat-freeze-protection-mi).

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator in a rental, or sets a rule for one the tenant supplies.

Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies, its dwelling classes assume cooking and kitchen accommodations for each family, each apartment in a Class A multiple dwelling is arranged to provide cooking accommodations and a kitchen sink within the unit, and a kitchen or cooking space for the common or joint use of the occupants of a 2-family or multiple dwelling is not allowed; those are design and use rules, not a duty to furnish appliances.

If you supply appliances, list them in the lease (appliances-included); you then maintain them under the lease and the covenants of fitness and repair, and a lease of less than 1 year cannot shift their repair to the tenant. To leave an item at the home that you will not supply, use the optional clause in appliances-excluded-mi.

When you take an old refrigerator out of service, remove its door latch or lock before leaving it anywhere children can reach: leaving one in that state is a misdemeanor.

For a federally assisted unit, HUD's national standards require a kitchen area with a sink, a cooking appliance, a refrigerator, food preparation space and food storage. Local ordinances may add requirements.

title: Shifting Repairs or Maintenance to the Tenant
bodyText:
In every Michigan residential lease you covenant that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended and that you will keep the premises in reasonable repair and comply with state and local health and safety laws.

The parties may modify those covenants, for example by making the tenant responsible for specified repairs or maintenance, only where the lease has a current term of at least 1 year. Michigan's statute asks nothing more: it sets no separate-writing, conspicuousness or consideration requirement and no list of duties that can or cannot be shifted.

In a month-to-month lease, a lease shorter than 1 year, or a 1-year lease after it continues on a periodic basis, no repair or fitness duty can be shifted to the tenant, and no lease of any length may waive or alter the tenant's remedies when the premises are unfit.

The library's clause for a lease of 1 year or more lists the specified items, keeps fitness, common areas and health and safety law compliance with you, and ends if the lease stops having a current term of at least 1 year (tenant-repair-agreement-mi). How far a court will let a modification reach is not settled by statute or by a published case the library has read.

Some duties are the tenant's by law and need no shift. Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies, tenants are responsible for the cleanliness of the parts of the premises they occupy and control, in a single-family or 2-family dwelling the occupants must provide, keep clean and in place covered garbage receptacles, and each occupant must comply with the provisions that apply specifically to the occupant.

Ordinary chores that are not repair or fitness duties, such as the yard care in the landscaping clause, are a matter of contract.

For a federal Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, the lease must say which utilities and appliances the family supplies, and the family can be held responsible for a housing quality breach caused by not paying those utilities or not maintaining those appliances.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText:
No Michigan statute says how a tenant must ask for repairs, whether a repair request must be written or may be oral, or that you must receive notice before your duty to repair arises.

Your covenants to keep the premises fit for the use intended and in reasonable repair carry no notice condition. In an eviction for nonpayment the court deducts rent excused by your breach of the lease or of those covenants, and no possession judgment enters for nonpayment where your breach excused the rent; neither rule turns on a written request.

Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies, an occupant may sue for damages from unsafe, unsanitary or unhealthful conditions after notice to you and a failure to correct them; the statute does not say the notice must be in writing.

A lease may ask the tenant to report conditions promptly in writing or through a set channel (the shared maintenance clause; the optional repair-requests-mi), and a record of requests helps you. But no lease may waive or alter the tenant's remedies when the premises are unfit, so do not treat a written request as a condition of those remedies or ignore a problem you learn of another way, such as a phone call, a text or your own inspection; a term that tried to do that risks being void.

The lease must state the name and address where notice under the Truth in Renting Act is given to you (lessor-notice-address-mi); that address is where a tenant sends written notice of a Truth in Renting violation, which you then have 20 days to cure before most suits, and it is not a limit on repair requests.

A tenant's complaint about a health or safety code violation to a government agency is protected against retaliation.

title: No Termination Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No Michigan statute lets you end a lease, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much, more than the rent or more than the home is worth (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution, 2025-2026 acts and the administrative rules in the library's corpus searched). Cost is not an exception to your covenants to keep the premises fit for the use intended and in reasonable repair. What Michigan does have: if the building is destroyed or made untenantable or unfit for occupancy without the tenant's fault or neglect, the tenant may quit and surrender possession and owes no rent after surrender, unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing (edu-casualty-mi). You have no statutory right to end the lease for that reason; for a lease with a term of at least 1 year the library offers an optional clause that lets you end it when the home is destroyed or cannot reasonably be repaired within a period you set (casualty-termination-mi), and for a shorter or periodic tenancy you end it only by the ordinary notice to quit (edu-casualty-short-term-mi, edu-termination-notice-mi). Repair cost against value appears in Michigan law only as a test for public enforcement: under the Housing Law a court may let the enforcing agency remove a building only if repair would cost more than its state equalized value (with exceptions for some urban core cities), and a local dangerous-building order to demolish follows the same comparison. Those are the local government's remedies, not a landlord's termination right. Ending a tenancy soon after a tenant has complained to a government agency about a code violation can be found retaliatory (edu-retaliation-mi).

title: No Rent Escrow Exemption Notice
bodyText: There is nothing for a Michigan landlord to give notice of here. No Michigan statute exempts a landlord from a tenant's rent escrow remedy because of how many units the landlord owns, and none provides an exemption notice (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution, 2025-2026 acts and the administrative rules in the library's corpus searched).
