No Michigan statute says whether an unemancipated minor's lease binds the minor, whether housing is a necessary the minor must pay for, or whether a minor who lied about age loses the right to back out (the statute barring that defense covers only goods and loans). Those are case-law questions the library has not read. Michigan's civil rights act bars refusing a rental or setting different terms because of age, and only hotels and bed and breakfasts have a statute letting them refuse a room to an unemancipated minor; whether the age rule reaches a refusal based on a minor's legal capacity to contract is also case law. The cautious course for an unemancipated applicant under 18 is not to refuse on age alone, to apply your usual screening, and, because the minor's own promise may not be enforceable, to have an adult sign as co-tenant or guarantor under a written policy you apply to every applicant who cannot contract, keeping the applicant's written statement of age. In an eviction, you sue the tenant or other person in possession; you need not name a minor child who is only an occupant, because the order of eviction removes all occupants (`edu-eviction-process-mi`). If a minor is a defendant, the court rules require service on the person who has care and control of the minor and lives with the minor, and the case may not proceed until the minor has a conservator or the court appoints a guardian ad litem. No Michigan statute otherwise bars filing against a minor or sets special eviction rules for minors. Federal law also bars requiring a tenant to vacate a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program until 30 days after a notice to vacate (`edu-cares-act-notice`).

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord in Court
bodyText: If you own your rentals in your own name, you may bring your own eviction or rent case: Michigan's Constitution gives every suitor the right to prosecute or defend a suit in person or by a lawyer. If the landlord is a corporation, limited liability company, partnership or other entity, plan on a licensed Michigan lawyer for an eviction or any other case in the district court's general civil division. No Michigan statute or court rule lets a non-lawyer, such as a member, manager, officer or property manager, appear in court for an entity in summary proceedings, and practicing law without a license is contempt of court. Whether a court will accept a non-lawyer's filing for an entity is case law. A property manager or other agent may still sign your demand for possession, which may be signed by the person entitled to possession, an attorney or an agent (`edu-nonpayment-notice-mi`). Small claims is the statutory exception, for money claims only up to $7,000 (it cannot order possession). There lawyers may not take part except on their own behalf; a sole proprietorship, partnership or corporation is represented by an officer or employee with direct and personal knowledge of the facts (or, if that person has left or is medically unavailable, by a supervisor, the proprietor, a partner, or a corporate officer or director); only the proprietor, a partner or a full-time salaried employee who knows the facts may file a claim for a proprietorship or partnership, and only a full-time salaried employee who knows the facts may file for a corporation; no one may file more than 5 claims a week in one district (the statute names proprietorships, partnerships and corporations but not limited liability companies, so ask the court how it treats an LLC); and an assignee, such as a collection agency that buys your claim, may not file there (`edu-landlord-remedies-termination-mi`). Two filing problems can stop an entity's case. A foreign (out-of-state) corporation, limited liability company or limited partnership that transacts business in Michigan without a Michigan certificate of authority or registration may not maintain a court action here until it gets one, although its leases stay valid and it may defend a suit; merely owning property is not transacting business, but whether renting it out is, is case law, so register before you file. And a person doing business under an assumed name without filing the county certificate, which covers individuals, partnerships, trusts, fiduciaries and other entities except corporations and limited partnerships, may not sue on contracts made under that name until it complies. Corporations file assumed names with the state under their own act; an LLC may file with the state, but the county act does not exclude LLCs and no text read says the state filing is enough, so an LLC using an assumed name should file both before suing. Federal law also bars requiring a tenant to vacate a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program until 30 days after a notice to vacate (`edu-cares-act-notice`).

title: Deadlines for Suing Over Rent and Damage
bodyText: Michigan has no limitation period written specifically for rent or leases, so the general periods apply. A suit for unpaid rent or other money due under a lease, written or oral, is a breach-of-contract action and must be brought within 6 years after the claim accrues. Each unpaid rent payment probably starts its own 6-year period when it falls due, since claims on an installment contract accrue as each installment falls due; whether a lease counts as an installment contract is case law, so sue within 6 years of the oldest unpaid payment. A claim for damage to the property brought as an injury to property rather than under the lease has 3 years. A judgment of the district court's general civil division can be enforced by a new action within 10 years (6 years for a small claims judgment), and the new judgment gets a new period. Several shorter deadlines matter more in practice: to keep any part of a security deposit for disputed damages you must file within 45 days after the occupancy ends (`edu-security-deposit-penalty-mi`); an eviction for a serious and continuing health hazard or extensive and continuing damage must be filed within 90 days after you discovered, or should have discovered, the condition; a tenant's complaint to a government agency or court within 90 days before you file raises a presumption of retaliation (`edu-retaliation-mi`); post-judgment motions and appeals in an eviction must be filed within 10 days; and an order of eviction must be issued within 56 days after judgment unless a hearing is held (`edu-eviction-process-mi`). A tenant who is locked out or otherwise unlawfully kept from possession must sue for possession within 90 days and for damages within 1 year (`edu-self-help-eviction-mi`). What restarts or stops the clock: a written acknowledgment of the debt or promise to pay, signed by the tenant, revives a barred claim or keeps it alive, but an oral promise does not; a receipt or note of payment written by you is not evidence of a part payment for this purpose, and what effect a part payment proved in other ways has is case law. Time a tenant spends outside Michigan, in stretches of more than 2 months, generally does not count unless you could have served the tenant while away, and the period stops running when you file, if the tenant is served within the time the court rules allow. If a tenant fraudulently conceals the claim or who is liable, you have 2 years after discovering it. A tenant's counterclaim is not barred by limitations, up to the amount of your claim, unless it was already barred when your claim arose. Sue well within the shortest period that could apply.

title: When You May Not Collect or Sue for Rent
bodyText: No Michigan statute generally bars you from demanding or collecting rent, raising rent, or serving a demand for possession because the home has code violations, has been cited, or lacks a local rental license. The limits are narrower. (1) Housing Law certificates: where the Housing Law of Michigan applies (`edu-housing-law-mi`, `edu-scope-mi`), the tenant's duty to pay rent under the lease is suspended while the premises have no required certificate of compliance or while an issued certificate is suspended, and the suspended rent is paid into an escrow account set up by the enforcing agency to pay for correcting the violations; the suspension does not start until you have had a reasonable time after notice of violations to apply for a temporary certificate, and does not apply if you show the occupant caused the hazard. If the tenant withholds rent but does not pay it into the escrow, you may sue for rent and possession, subject to the tenant's defenses; rent paid into that escrow, under a court repair order, or to a court-appointed receiver is a defense to a nonpayment eviction. In a Housing Law enforcement case the court may also let a tenant who did not cause the violation repair it and deduct the cost from rent. (2) Public assistance rent: if the state refuses to pay a public-assistance rent grant because a building or housing official found the unit fails the code through your fault, you may not sue for that rent or for possession while the refusal lasts; if the defects are corrected or the refusal is found wrongful, the state pays the rent withheld. If you take part in the state's rent vendoring program, you may not evict a tenant based solely on the state ending your participation because of a housing code hazard (`edu-no-benefit-delay-defense-mi`). (3) In every eviction for nonpayment, the court deducts any rent excused by your breach of the lease or of your duty to keep the home fit and in reasonable repair, and your breach that excuses rent is a defense to possession; a lease cannot take those remedies away (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-mi`, `edu-habitability-mi`). A newly built or altered building generally may not be occupied until the building department issues a certificate of use and occupancy. Many cities require rental registration or inspection and may attach rent or eviction consequences to it; those are local ordinances, which the library does not cover.

title: Renting the Same Home Twice
bodyText: No Michigan statute forbids renting the same home or room to two tenants for the same period, or says which of two competing tenants is entitled to it, and Michigan has no general statute giving a tenant a remedy when you fail to deliver possession on the start date (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The library's possession-delay clause (`possession-delay`, used in Michigan leases) covers only a delay that is not your fault: rent abates until you deliver, and the tenant may end the lease and get everything back if you have not delivered within 30 days. Letting the same home twice is your fault, so the tenant who loses out keeps the ordinary remedies for your breach of the lease. Michigan's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases, and taking rent, a deposit or a fee for a home already promised to someone else may be an unfair or deceptive practice; a tenant who suffers a loss from a violation may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees (`edu-consumer-protection-mi`). Which competing tenant wins, and what the other may recover, are case-law questions the library has not read. Keep one signed lease per home and period, do not take a second application fee or deposit for a home already promised, and if two leases overlap, refund the second tenant at once. Whoever is in possession can be removed only through the courts, never by changing the locks (`edu-self-help-eviction-mi`).

title: Barring Non-Tenants Under Trespass Law
bodyText:
You can use Michigan's trespass law to keep a person who is not your tenant off your rental property, within limits. A person commits misdemeanor trespass who, without lawful authority, enters the lands or premises of another after being forbidden to do so by the owner or occupant or the owner's or occupant's agent, or remains after being told to leave by one of them; the penalty is up to 30 days in jail, a fine of up to $250, or both. A process server attempting service by the most direct route is excepted.

Because the statute lets the occupant as well as the owner give or withhold permission, your tenant is an occupant who may invite people to the tenant's own home, and whether a tenant's invitation gives a person you have barred lawful authority to come to the unit, or through the common areas to it, is case law.

So give a barred non-tenant written notice not to enter the property and keep a copy, ask the police to act on it in areas you control, and pair it with a lease covenant that makes your tenant keep that person away, enforceable as a lease breach (optional clause `barred-person-covenant-ne`).

Bar people only for their conduct, never for a protected characteristic, and do not use a barring notice against a person your tenant must admit by law or court order, or against someone your tenant is seeking protection from.

None of this removes a tenant or former tenant, who must be evicted through the courts. A person who took possession by forcible entry or by trespass without color of title or other possessory interest may be removed by a summary proceeding, or by peaceable re-entry.

As a possessor of land you generally owe a trespasser no duty to make the property safe, with exceptions for willful and wanton misconduct, a known trespasser and certain conditions that attract children. Local ordinances may add rules; the library does not cover them.

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan has no statute that creates a special seasonal tenancy, exempts a seasonal lease from the eviction rules, or prescribes a seasonal lease form (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). A seasonal rental is an ordinary fixed-term tenancy: it ends on its end date without notice, and a tenant who stays is removed by summary proceedings, never by a lockout (`edu-eviction-process-mi`, `edu-holdover-mi`). Seasonal status matters for coverage. The Truth in Renting Act's lease rules do not apply to a hotel, motel, motor home or other tourist accommodation used as a temporary accommodation for guests or tourists, or to your own principal residence rented occasionally while you are away, for example on vacation or sabbatical (`edu-scope-mi`). Those exceptions are narrow: a cottage or apartment rented for a season to someone who lives there is residential premises, and the Truth in Renting Act, the security deposit act (which covers any rental unit used as a home, residence or sleeping unit) and your repair covenants apply as in any other lease. Taxes: Michigan's use tax applies to rooms or lodging furnished by those who offer accommodations to the public as a commercial enterprise, including tourist homes and resort lodges and cabins, except rooms and lodging rented for a continuous period of more than 1 month; local accommodation taxes may also apply. Check with a tax adviser. Campgrounds have their own statute: the operator may remove an occupant who disturbs the peace, damages the facilities or does not pay the agreed rent, after a written request to leave stating the reasons and refunding any unused advance payment, and staying after that request is a misdemeanor; a written lease may add grounds. Seasonal mobile home parks are regulated separately and are outside this library. Many cities and townships regulate short-term rentals by ordinance; the library does not cover local ordinances.

title: Tenant Absences and Abandonment
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, or requires your lease to ask.

You may require it in the lease: the optional absence-notice clause (`extended-absence-notice-ks`) asks the tenant to tell you, by the first day, of any absence of more than 7 consecutive days, and lets you recover your actual damages for a willful failure.

An absence notice matters most for abandonment. You may retake possession without a court order only if you believe in good faith that the tenant has abandoned the home, have reason to believe after diligent inquiry that the tenant does not intend to return, and current rent is unpaid; otherwise even a long absence is not abandonment, and the tenant may recover damages of at least $200 for each unlawful interference (`abandoned-property-mi`). A tenant who has told you of an absence has told you that the tenant intends to return, so do not treat the home as abandoned during a notified absence.

If you believe a sole tenant has died, follow the statutory procedure.

An absence gives you no extra right of entry: enter as your lease's entry terms allow, and where the Housing Law applies you must request and obtain the tenant's permission except in an emergency such as fire or flood (`landlords-access-mi`). Local ordinances may add rules; the library does not cover them.

title: A Tenant's Statutory Rights to End the Lease Early
bodyText:
Michigan law lets a residential tenant end a lease, or stop owing rent, early on a few statutory grounds. Your lease's own early-termination option (`early-termination-ks`) is separate, must leave these rights intact, and may not charge a fee for using them.

(1) Senior housing or incapacity: every rental agreement must let a tenant who has occupied the unit for more than 13 months end the lease by 60 days' written notice if, during the term, the tenant becomes eligible to move into subsidized senior citizen housing and gives you written proof, or becomes unable to live independently, as a physician certifies in a notarized statement (`early-termination-senior-infirmity-mi`). The statute does not say what follows if a lease leaves this out; the library's clause includes it.

(2) Domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking: a tenant with a reasonable apprehension of present danger to the tenant or the tenant's child who sends written notice by certified mail with the required documentation is released from rent no later than the first day of the second month that rent is due after the notice, but not before moving out; prepaid rent is not refunded and co-tenants stay bound.

(3) Untenantable building: if the building is destroyed or made untenantable or unfit for occupancy without the tenant's fault or neglect, the tenant may quit and surrender possession and owes no rent after surrender, unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing.

(4) Condominium conversion: a tenant who receives the developer's conversion notice may end the tenancy at any time by giving the developer at least 60 days' notice.

(5) Prohibited lease terms: if your lease contains a term the Truth in Renting Act prohibits and you do not cure it within 20 days after the tenant's written notice (or without notice in some cases), the tenant may sue to void the lease and end the tenancy, and recover damages.

(6) Military service (federal law): a servicemember who enters military service after signing, or who receives permanent change-of-station or deployment orders of at least 90 days, or a stop-movement order of at least 30 days after signing on receipt of such orders, may end a residential lease by written notice with a copy of the orders; for monthly rent the lease ends 30 days after the next rent due date following the notice, rent is prorated, and you may not charge an early termination fee. A spouse or dependent may end the lease within a year after a servicemember dies in service, and a servicemember with a catastrophic injury or illness may do so within a year.

A periodic tenant may also end the tenancy by the ordinary notice.

No Michigan statute lets a tenant end a lease because you misrepresented the property, or because of a job transfer, illness or age outside the 13-month rule; those exits, if any, come from the lease or from case law.

title: No Statutory Exit After an Environmental Event
bodyText: No Michigan statute gives you, or your tenant, a right to end a lease because a flood, storm, contamination, public health emergency, disaster or government vacate order makes the home unusable (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The tenant's statutory exit is broader than the event list: if the building is destroyed or so injured by the elements or in any other way that it is untenantable or unfit for occupancy, and the tenant was not at fault, the tenant may move out and owes no rent after surrendering possession, unless you and the tenant agreed otherwise in writing (`edu-casualty-mi`). You have no statutory right to end the lease. Your duty to keep the home fit and in reasonable repair runs for the whole term and may be changed only in a lease of at least 1 year. For a lease of at least 1 year, the library's optional casualty clause (`casualty-termination-mi`) lets you end the lease if the home is destroyed by fire, storm or other casualty, or damaged by one so that it is unfit to live in and cannot reasonably be repaired within a period you set, while keeping the tenant's statutory right; the library offers no broader environmental-event termination clause for Michigan. Where the Housing Law applies (`edu-housing-law-mi`), the enforcing agency may order occupied premises vacated while a certificate of compliance is withheld or suspended, the tenant's rent is suspended into escrow (`edu-rent-demand-bar-mi`), and a court may issue an order of eviction immediately after judgment if the premises have been ordered vacated for lack of a certificate. A home found contaminated by methamphetamine manufacture has its own rules (`edu-meth-mi`). Whether rent is owed while a government order bars occupancy outside these rules is a contract question the library has not resolved.

title: Move-Out Forms and Work During a Notice
bodyText: No Michigan statute governs a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, requires a warning if the form adds terms, or sets what a tenant's notice of intent to vacate must say (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched; the statutes that use the phrase notice to vacate concern government relocation). A periodic tenant ends the tenancy by the ordinary notice (`edu-tenancy-at-will-mi`). Rules that still matter: a lease may not let you change its terms after it starts without the tenant's written consent, so a signed form can change the lease, but a term the Truth in Renting Act or the security deposit act bars is void however it is signed, the deposit act's requirements cannot be waived, and under the Consumer Protection Act a waiver of a legal right counts only if it is clearly stated and the tenant specifically consents (`edu-truth-in-renting-mi`, `edu-consumer-protection-mi`). Keep a move-out form to the facts: the move-out date and the tenant's forwarding address. The tenant must give you a forwarding address in writing within 4 days after moving out; if the tenant does not, you need not send the notice of damages, though the tenant may still claim the deposit (`security-deposit-return-mi`). Put any new term in a separate written amendment that says it changes the lease, and do not use the form to add a charge. Until the tenancy ends, your duties continue: keep the home fit and in reasonable repair, and do not interfere with the tenant's possession. Interrupting heat, water, hot water, electricity or gas, introducing noise, odor or another nuisance, removing doors, windows or locks, or boarding up the premises is unlawful interference, for which the tenant may recover at least $200 per occurrence; you may interfere only temporarily, as necessary to make needed repairs or inspections as the law allows (`edu-self-help-eviction-mi`). Enter only as your lease allows, and where the Housing Law applies only with the tenant's permission except in an emergency (`landlords-access-mi`). Do not start renovation that makes the home unfit while the tenant still lives there.

title: Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a lease disclosure when you submeter or resell electricity or natural gas to a tenant, and none sets rules for landlord submetering (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution, 2025-2026 acts and the Public Service Commission's residential service rules searched). Three statutes make landlord submetering of electricity doubtful, so the cautious course is not to do it. First, only investor-owned, cooperative or municipally owned electric utilities may own or operate electric meter equipment used in distributing electricity, although the same law leaves in place any existing right of a non-utility to run a private distribution system on private property. Second, a person that owns or operates equipment for delivering or furnishing gas or electricity to or for the public for compensation is a public utility, which needs the Commission's certificate before serving where another utility already serves; no statute says whether a landlord billing only its own tenants serves the public. Third, a meter you use to figure a tenant's charge is not a meter regulated and tested as part of a public utility system, so it appears to be a commercial measuring device under the Weights and Measures Act, which must hold a certificate of conformance and meet the national technical standards the Act adopts. Until the Commission's orders and the utilities' tariffs say otherwise, have each tenant hold the account for a utility-owned meter that serves only the unit, or include the electricity or gas in the rent. EV charging is treated differently: a provider of electric vehicle charging services is not a public utility and may charge by the kilowatt-hour (edu-ev-charging-requirements-mi). Mobile home parks may charge for electric, fuel or water service only if each resident's use is first accurately and consistently measured, unless the service is included in the rent. For water, sewer and trash bills shared among units, see utility-apportionment-mi; related: edu-no-submetering-rule-mi.

title: On-Bill Energy Project Charges
bodyText:
Michigan has no meter conservation charge requiring a notice to each new tenant, and no statute requires you to tell a tenant about an energy charge on the meter, but Michigan does have on-bill energy project charges that stay with the property.

A utility whose rates the Public Service Commission regulates may run a residential energy projects program, and a city, village or township served by a municipal electric utility may run a residential clean energy program. Under either, a record owner's loan for an energy project (such as insulation, windows, heating and cooling equipment, wiring for EV charging, or a renewable energy system) is repaid through a per-meter charge on the utility bill for the property.

If notice of the loan is recorded with the register of deeds, the duty to pay the per-meter charge runs with the land and binds future customers who contract for service to the property, which includes a tenant who opens the account in the tenant's own name, and the utility may shut off service for nonpayment of the charge as it would for any other charge.

Because a tenant could not reasonably know of such a charge, disclose it before signing: failing to reveal a material fact of that kind is an unfair practice under the Consumer Protection Act, and a lease term that violates that Act is barred. The library's optional clause meter-project-charge-disclosure-mi discloses the charge and says who pays it.

Michigan has no statute on submetered water either; a water submeter you use to figure a tenant's charge raises the same Weights and Measures Act question as an electric one (utility-apportionment-mi).

title: Utility Allowances and Rebilled Utilities
bodyText:
No Michigan statute caps what you may charge a tenant when you pass on a utility bill, or regulates utility allowances in private rentals. Mobile home parks are the exception: a park may charge for electric, fuel or water service only if each resident's use is first accurately and consistently measured, unless the service is included in the rent.

For other rentals, charge only the provider's actual bill, with no markup or added fee, and give the tenant a copy of the bill.

An allowance set in the lease at signing, with the tenant paying the provider's actual charge above it, is a lease term, not a change during the term; raising the rent during the term because utility costs went up is allowed only on at least 30 days' written notice under rent-cost-adjustment-mi.

Use an allowance for electricity or gas only where a utility-owned meter serves only the unit; for a water, sewer or trash bill shared with other units use utility-apportionment-mi. A utility bill the tenant leaves unpaid may be taken from the security deposit under the deposit rules (security-deposit-use-mi).

Never shut off service to collect a utility charge: causing the interruption of heat, water, electricity or gas that the tenant procured or that you must furnish is unlawful interference with possession. The library's optional allowance clause is utility-allowance-cap-mi.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText:
No Michigan statute bars a lease term that makes a tenant pay for a utility not separately metered to the unit, or sets how you split a shared bill among units, whether by submeter, floor area, number of occupants or another formula.

Four rules shape it. First, for electricity and natural gas the cautious course is not to allocate or submeter at all.

Second, a submeter you use to figure a tenant's charge for water or another service is not a utility-regulated meter, so it appears to be a commercial measuring device that needs a certificate of conformance under the Weights and Measures Act; dividing the bill by a stated formula avoids that question.

Third, municipal water and sewer charges can become a lien on your property even if the tenant is responsible for them, unless you take the steps the statute for your system requires (a lease provision and affidavit, or written notice to the governing body with a copy of the lease); see municipal-water-lien-mi.

Fourth, mobile home parks may charge for electric, fuel or water service only if each resident's use is first accurately and consistently measured, unless the service is included in the rent.

For water, sewer, storm water and trash in other rentals, the optional clause utility-apportionment-mi states the method, passes through only what the provider bills and gives the tenant a copy of each bill. Tell the tenant before signing how the share is figured: failing to reveal a material fact the tenant could not reasonably know is an unfair practice under the Consumer Protection Act. Never shut off service to collect a share.

title: No Required Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a lease to include a utility disclosure or attachment, such as a list of the utilities the tenant pays, the providers, average costs or whether service is available (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution, 2025-2026 acts and the Public Service Commission's residential service rules searched). What the lease says still matters. An occupant must open an account with an electric or gas utility the Commission regulates within 30 business days of taking occupancy, unless residential service is included in a lease, so the lease should say plainly which utilities you provide and which the tenant must put in the tenant's own name (utilities-paid-by-landlord, utilities-responsibility, utility-transfer-nj). A fact about utilities that the tenant could not reasonably know, such as a charge you bill yourself, a shared bill or an energy project charge on the meter, should be disclosed before signing to avoid a Consumer Protection Act claim (utility-apportionment-mi, meter-project-charge-disclosure-mi). Mobile home parks may charge for electric, fuel or water service only if each resident's use is first accurately and consistently measured, unless the service is included in the rent.

title: Naming the Landlord for Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
For electric and natural gas utilities the Public Service Commission regulates, the utility must let a customer name a consenting person or agency to receive a copy of any shutoff notice, and a customer may designate a third party to receive bills, shutoff notices or other communications by giving the utility a document signed by both the customer and the third party.

A tenant who holds the account can therefore name you, with your consent, to receive copies of shutoff notices. Receiving bills as a third party does not make you responsible for them unless you have signed on as a guarantor.

The shared optional clause utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co applies in Michigan as written: the tenant authorizes you as a contact and agrees to sign the utility's form, which you sign too.

Municipally owned utilities are outside the Commission's rules. The statute on shutoffs by municipally owned electric and gas utilities has no designee provision, and no statute read covers municipal water or sewer notices, so ask the utility.

Separately, when a building used by 3 or more households is on a single meter in your name, the utility must notify each unit at least 30 days before shutting off service for your unpaid bill. Receiving notices gives you no right to shut off service yourself.

title: Utility Interruptions and Submetered Service
bodyText: Michigan has no separate rule for interrupting electricity or gas you submeter or resell to a tenant, because no statute sets up landlord submetering, and the cautious course is not to submeter (edu-electric-submetering-mi). The general rule covers every utility you supply or the tenant procures: causing, by action or omission, the termination or interruption of a service so essential that losing it would be a constructive eviction, including heat, running water, hot water, electricity or gas, is unlawful interference with possession, whether you must furnish the service or the tenant procured it. The tenant may recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence, and possession, and the lease cannot waive this. You are protected only when you act under a court order; interfere temporarily only as necessary to make needed repairs or inspection and only as provided by law; believe in good faith, after diligent inquiry, that the tenant has abandoned the premises and does not intend to return and current rent is not paid; or follow the deceased-tenant procedure (or the occupant took possession by force or trespass). So never shut off, or ask a provider to discontinue, a utility to collect rent or a utility charge or to make a tenant move out. When an electric or gas account is in your name, a utility the Public Service Commission regulates may not shut off service because you did not pay for service a tenant used unless, after proper notice, you give a notarized statement that the premises are unoccupied, the occupant agrees in writing, or serving the occupant directly is not feasible without a major revision of facilities; where it is feasible, the utility must offer the occupant service in the occupant's own name, and if the occupant refuses, the utility may shut off service (edu-utility-landlord-account-mi). Municipally owned electric and gas utilities are bound by the same rule by statute. When a utility supplies a licensed mobile home park for the use of its tenants, the utility must notify the state department 10 days before shutting off service for nonpayment.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Michigan's utility shutoff protections belong to the utility's customer, so they protect a tenant who holds the account, and you when the account is in your name. For electric and natural gas utilities the Public Service Commission regulates: the utility must mail or deliver a shutoff notice at least 10 days before shutting off and make at least 2 attempts to reach the customer before an involuntary shutoff; shutoff may happen only between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m., and not on a day, or the day before a day, when the utility cannot restore service. During the heating season (November 1 through March 31) the utility may not shut off an eligible senior citizen customer (65 or older), and an eligible low-income customer who pays 7% of the estimated annual bill each month and shows within 14 days of asking for protection that the customer has applied for heating assistance is protected, with any past-due balance spread over the following months. A medical emergency certified on the Commission's form postpones shutoff for up to 21 days at a time, up to 63 days per household member in 12 months. An eligible military customer is protected for 90 days, with at least one more 90-day period on request. Each utility must also have an approved policy for suspending disconnections in extreme hot and cold weather. Municipally owned utilities follow their own statutes: 10 days' notice, postponement for a certified medical emergency, and, for municipal electric utilities, the same heating-season protection for seniors and low-income customers. Michigan has no blanket winter moratorium, no extra notice period added in winter, and no rule tied to a declared storm emergency. None of this lets you shut off a utility yourself (edu-utility-interruption-mi); when the account is in your name, see edu-utility-landlord-account-mi.

title: Moving Utility Accounts Into the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
No Michigan statute sets a deadline for a tenant to move a utility account into the tenant's name, or lets you cut off service the tenant has not transferred.

For electric and natural gas utilities the Commission regulates, an occupant must open an account within 30 business days of taking occupancy, unless residential service is included in a lease. If the customer of record moves out while another occupant stays, the customer must tell the utility, the occupant must open an account within 30 days, and the utility may hold the occupant responsible for service used after the customer left, billing back no more than 24 months.

If you hold the account and want to close it while a tenant lives there, you must tell the utility that an occupant continues to occupy the premises; the utility may not shut off service for your unpaid bill for service a tenant used unless you give a notarized statement that the premises are unoccupied, the occupant agrees in writing, or serving the occupant directly is not feasible, and where it is feasible it must first offer the occupant service in the occupant's own name; if the occupant refuses, the utility may shut off service. Municipally owned electric and gas utilities follow the same rule by statute.

For a city or township water or sewer account, unpaid charges can become a lien on your property even when the tenant ran them up unless you take the steps the statute requires ( edu-municipal-water-lien-mi, municipal-water-lien-mi).

Do not ask a utility to stop service to make a tenant transfer an account: causing the interruption of heat, water, electricity or gas is unlawful interference with possession.

The shared utility-transfer-nj clause applies in Michigan as written: the tenant transfers each account by a date you set, reimburses the provider's actual charges for any period an account stays in your name, and you promise not to cut off service.

title: EV Charging at Michigan Rentals
bodyText:
Michigan gives tenants no right to install EV charging and sets no lease terms for it, but four statutes matter if you let a tenant charge or charge tenants for it.

First, a provider of electric vehicle charging services is not a public utility, may own and operate a charging station, and may not be barred from charging by the kilowatt-hour; a utility that sells charging stays regulated.

Second, a charger or meter you use to figure what a tenant owes is not a meter regulated as part of a public utility system, so it appears to be a commercial measuring device under the Weights and Measures Act, which must hold a certificate of conformance and meet the national technical standards the Act adopts; the library has not read those standards or the state's practice for chargers at rentals.

Third, no Michigan tax applies only to electricity sold through an EV charger; electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles pay higher registration taxes instead, and whether general sales tax reaches charging you sell to a tenant has not been researched.

Fourth, if you own a condominium unit or a home in an association, the Homeowners' Energy Policy Act voids association rules that bar, or require approval for, installing electric vehicle supply equipment at your home or unit, but not in a common area; the right is yours as the owner, not your tenant's.

The simplest course is to have a tenant's charger run on the electric service the utility meters and bills in the tenant's name. The library's optional clause ev-charger-installation-mi lets a tenant install a charger with your written consent; it replaces, in Michigan, the shared ev-charger-installation-hi clause, whose electricity charge by a landlord meter or calculation does not fit these rules.

title: EV Charging Equipment When the Lease Ends
bodyText: No Michigan statute decides who owns EV charging equipment a tenant installed when the tenancy ends, or whether the tenant may or must remove it (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The lease decides. Under the library's Michigan EV clause (ev-charger-installation-mi) the equipment stays the tenant's, and the tenant removes it and repairs damage its installation or removal caused, other than ordinary wear and tear, unless you both agree in writing that it stays and on what terms. Under the shared No Alterations clause, an alteration you approve otherwise stays with the property unless you require its removal. Unpaid repair costs can come from the security deposit only for actual damage beyond normal living, itemized as the deposit rules require (security-deposit-use-mi). The shared clause ev-charging-end-of-tenancy-co, written for Colorado's statute, is not used in Michigan.

title: EV Charging in Shared Parking Areas
bodyText: No Michigan statute gives a tenant a right to install EV charging in a shared parking area, or sets the terms if you allow it (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The Homeowners' Energy Policy Act, which stops associations from barring electric vehicle supply equipment at an owner's home or unit, does not apply in a common area or on a shared roof. If you agree to a tenant's charger in a shared lot, use ev-charger-installation-mi, which names the space and requires your written consent and a written agreement on how the charger's electricity is paid for; assign the space in writing (assigned-parking-space-mi). Any extra rent for the space must be agreed in writing when you allow the charger, since a new charge cannot be added later by notice. The shared clause ev-charging-shared-area-co, which lets you charge an unstated reasonable fee to reserve the space, is not used in Michigan.

title: Cable, Satellite and Internet Access
bodyText:
No Michigan statute gives a cable, satellite or internet provider access to a rental building, gives a tenant a right to choose a provider, or bars charging subscribers a different rent.

Federal law does reach your lease. The FCC's over-the-air reception devices rule bars a lease provision that impairs a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or fixed wireless antenna one meter or less in diameter, a TV broadcast antenna, or a mast supporting one, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a balcony or patio.

A restriction impairs if it unreasonably delays or prevents installation, maintenance or use, unreasonably increases its cost, or prevents an acceptable signal; a restriction needed for a clearly defined safety objective that is written down and applied alike to comparable fixtures, or needed to preserve a site listed on or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, is allowed if it is no more burdensome than necessary.

The rule does not give a tenant a right to install on a roof, an exterior wall or other areas outside the tenant's exclusive use.

In a mobile home park, the park may not bar an exterior TV antenna on a home, subject to reasonable rules on location, size and style, unless it gives residents a central antenna free of charge.

The shared telecom-access-mn clause applies in Michigan as written: it requires your consent before drilling or installing, makes installers the tenant's guests, requires removal and repair at the end, and yields to any federal right.

title: Plug-In and Portable Solar Devices
bodyText: Michigan gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or portable solar device, and no statute voids a lease term restricting solar equipment (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The Homeowners' Energy Policy Act voids association rules that prohibit solar energy systems or require approval for energy-saving improvements, but it protects members of a homeowners' association, who are owners, and does not apply in a common area or on a shared roof; if you own a unit in an association the right is yours, not your tenant's. Under the shared No Alterations clause a tenant needs your written consent to attach equipment to the property. Utility approval is the other question: under the state's distributed generation program for utilities whose rates the Public Service Commission regulates, utility testing and approval of the interconnection, including all metering, and a signed parallel operating agreement must come before equipment is operated in parallel with the utility's system. Whether that reaches a small device plugged into a household outlet turns on utility tariffs and Commission rules the library has not read. For that reason the library does not offer a Michigan plug-in solar clause; you may allow a device by written consent, or add your own clause after taking advice, and the cautious course is to allow one only after the account holder has the utility's written approval.

title: Renter Property Tax Credit and Rent Statements
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires you to give a tenant a statement of the part of the rent that goes to property taxes, or to certify the rent a tenant paid (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan renters can claim the homestead property tax credit on their state income tax return, figured on 23% of the gross rent paid (10% for housing that pays a service charge in lieu of property taxes under the state housing development authority act), and only the renter may claim the credit on rented property. Gross rent is the total rent contracted to be paid in an arm's-length deal; if the deal is not at arm's length, the Department of Treasury may adjust it. Site rent for a mobile home in a park counts as rent. Raising a tenant's rent because the tenant claims and receives the credit is a misdemeanor, and so is giving tenants who do not claim it a lower rent. A rent increase during the term to cover higher property taxes is a different matter, allowed only on at least 30 days' written notice under rent-cost-adjustment-mi. A written record of rent paid, such as receipts or a year-end statement, helps a tenant claim the credit, though no statute requires it.

title: Parking Rules and Towing Signs
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires parking or towing rules to be delivered before signing, prescribes a heading for them, limits the vehicle information you may ask for, ties a parking permit to the lease term, or requires the lease to state whether parking is provided and what it costs. Two general rules control.

First, once the lease starts you may not change its terms, parking rules and parking charges included, without the tenant's written consent, except that the lease may reserve your right to make, on at least 30 days' written notice, a change required by federal, state or local law, rule or regulation, or a change in rules relating to the property that is required to protect the physical health, safety or peaceful enjoyment of tenants and guests. So put parking rules and any parking charge in the lease or a rules attachment at signing (rules-mi, parking-vehicle-rules-mi, assigned-parking-space-mi).

Second, towing: a property owner may have a vehicle taken into custody as abandoned only if it has remained on the property without the owner's consent, through a local towing agency that must notify the police first; a tenant's or occupant's vehicle parked under the lease is not such a vehicle, and removing it without a court order risks a claim for unlawful interference with possession.

Before you authorize towing a vehicle without its owner's consent, you must post a sign at each vehicle entrance (on property without curbs or barriers, at least 1 for each 100 feet of road frontage), in letters at least 2 inches high on a contrasting background, saying unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense and giving the towing service's name and phone number, permanently installed with its bottom at least 4 feet above the ground and kept up for at least 24 hours before any tow. The sign rule does not apply to property that is part of a single- or two-family home, or where the vehicle's owner is personally told that the area is reserved and the vehicle may be towed.

Michigan has no separate waiting period for vehicles with expired registration. Local ordinances may add requirements.

title: Parking Priced Separately From Rent
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires you to price parking separately from the rent (unbundled parking), or bars including it in the rent. You may include parking in the rent or offer it for a separate charge. Either way, set the space and any separate charge in the lease at signing (assigned-parking-space-mi, unbundled-parking-mi): a new or higher parking charge during the term needs the tenant's written consent.

The optional clause unbundled-parking-mi lets a tenant who rents without parking add a space for a fixed monthly charge that does not rise during the term, and lets either side end the arrangement on written notice. Local ordinances or zoning approvals may regulate parking for new buildings.

title: Entry for Periodic Services: Michigan Rules
bodyText:
Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies (cities, villages and townships of 10,000 or more, and for single-family and 2-family homes only places of 100,000 or more unless the local body adopts it), you must request and obtain the tenant's permission before entering the leasehold, except in an emergency such as fire, flood or another threat of serious injury or death.

The statute does not say whether a lease term can give that permission in advance for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes, pest treatment or alarm checks, so the cautious course is to ask permission before each visit, scheduled services included.

Outside those places no Michigan statute sets an entry notice period or requires a scheduled-services term to be conspicuous or separately signed. Anywhere, an entry may not become unlawful interference with possession.

The optional clause scheduled-services-entry-mi lists each service and its schedule, sets the hours, gives advance notice of each visit, asks permission each time and has the tenant agree not to refuse unreasonably; the shared scheduled-services-entry-la clause, which allows entry on notice alone, is not used in Michigan. General entry: landlords-access-mi.

title: No Automatic-Renewal Statute; Renewal Terms in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute regulates an automatic-renewal clause in a residential lease. Nothing requires larger or bold type, a separate signature or opt-in, or a reminder notice before the lease renews, and nothing limits how early you may ask a tenant to decide whether to renew. The automatic-renewal rules Michigan does have govern other contracts, such as personnel agency contracts and rental-purchase agreements for household goods, not leases of homes.

The Truth in Renting Act still shapes a renewal clause. A Michigan lease may not let you change any of its terms after the tenancy starts without the tenant's written consent, except three adjustments the lease provides for on at least 30 days' written notice.

So a renewal clause should renew the lease on its existing terms, or on terms fixed when the lease is signed. A different rent or other change for a renewal term needs a new written agreement signed by the tenant, or one of the three allowed adjustments; a clause letting you set a new rent for the renewal by notice alone risks being void, with the tenant's remedies under the Act.

If the lease renews month to month, either of you may end it with the ordinary notice, and you may then offer a new lease on new terms.

A lease for longer than 1 year is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by you or an agent you authorized in writing, so keep the renewal clause in the signed lease.

A renewal also carries the statutory terms that apply to leases entered into, renewed or renegotiated, including the tenant's early termination right for senior housing or infirmity (`early-termination-senior-infirmity-mi`) and the domestic violence release. The library's optional Michigan clause is `automatic-renewal-mi`.

title: Lease Guarantors and Renewals in Michigan
bodyText:
Michigan has no statute on lease guarantors. Nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a guaranty to state renewal terms, a maximum amount or an end date, lets a guarantor make you sue the tenant first, or says whether a guarantor may revoke a guaranty as to future rent.

Two general rules apply. (1) A special promise to answer for the debt, default or misdoings of another person is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor, so have the guarantor sign the lease or a written guaranty.

(2) Michigan's cosigner law may reach a person who signs, without being paid for it, to answer for the tenant's rent. Before you report adverse information about a cosigner to a credit bureau, give information about the cosigned obligation to a collection agency, or take any collection action against the cosigner (which includes asking the cosigner to pay), you must mail the cosigner, by first-class mail, a notice that the tenant is delinquent or in default and that the cosigner is responsible for payment, and allow at least 30 days from the date it was sent to pay the amount then due or make other arrangements satisfactory to you. If the cosigner does that, you may not report adverse information. A cosigner who suffers loss from a violation may recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees, after giving you 30 days' notice and a chance to make it good.

That law covers debts for personal, family or household purposes and does not cover a person who has executed a guarantee; whether a lease guaranty is such a guarantee, and whether unpaid rent is such a debt, is case law, so follow the notice steps for every guarantor or co-signer.

Whether a guaranty covers a renewal, extension or month-to-month continuation depends on its words, and how a court reads silence is case law, so say so in the guaranty, as the library's optional clause does (`guaranty-mi`).

The security deposit cap of 1 1/2 months' rent is written for deposits paid by the tenant; whether a deposit you take from a guarantor counts toward it is not settled by statute, so count it. If you hold 5 or more units, apply any guarantor requirement the same way whatever an applicant's lawful source of income.

title: No Landlord Foreclosure Disclosure Statute in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires you, as the landlord, to tell a tenant or an applicant that the property is in default or foreclosure, before or after the lease is signed.

Tenants usually learn of a foreclosure from others. In a mortgage foreclosure by advertisement, notice of the sale is published for 4 weeks and a copy must be posted in a conspicuous place on the premises within 15 days after the first publication.

In a property tax foreclosure, the foreclosing government must visit each forfeited property; if it appears occupied, it must try to serve an occupant personally with notice of the hearings, tell the occupant that the property will be foreclosed and the occupants will have to vacate unless the taxes are paid, and, if it does not meet an occupant, post a plain-English notice on the property.

If your lender holds an assignment of rents, it may notify the tenant to pay rent to it, and after a foreclosure, federal law generally lets a bona fide tenant whose lease began before the notice of foreclosure stay until the lease ends, subject to exceptions such as a sale to a buyer who will live there, and requires at least 90 days' notice to vacate.

Michigan's Consumer Protection Act, which reaches leases, makes it unlawful to fail to reveal a material fact whose omission tends to mislead or deceive the consumer and which the consumer could not reasonably know. Whether a pending foreclosure is such a fact for someone about to sign a lease is case law, so the cautious course is to tell an applicant in writing before signing if foreclosure proceedings have begun; the library's disclosure clause records that statement (`foreclosure-disclosure-nv`).

title: Notice of Lawsuits and Proceedings Affecting the Property in Michigan
bodyText:
Michigan has no general rule requiring you to tell tenants or applicants that the property faces a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax foreclosure, condemnation or code-enforcement case, and no rule requiring a tenant to tell you when the tenant receives such a notice.

Tenants often hear from others instead. A mortgage foreclosure sale notice is posted on the premises, and in a property tax foreclosure the foreclosing government visits occupied property to serve or post notice. In a condemnation, when the taking might require relocation, the agency must give the occupants written notice that an eminent domain proceeding has begun and of their basic rights, including the moving allowance and the time to relocate. A lender with an assignment of rents may tell the tenant to pay rent to it. Code-enforcement orders generally go to the owner, though where the Housing Law applies the enforcing agency notifies occupants in writing of a serious and imminent hazard and may order occupied premises vacated.

Because papers addressed to the owner or to "Occupant" often arrive at the rental, a lease term asking the tenant to pass them on promptly is lawful and useful; the library's optional clause does this without making the tenant responsible for the matter or limiting any right the tenant has (`adverse-proceeding-notice-mi`).

title: Eminent Domain and Residential Leases in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute says what happens to a residential lease when the property is taken by eminent domain: none ends the lease or the rent, lets the court cancel the lease, makes the lease's own condemnation terms control, or lets either side end the lease after a partial taking. Those questions are left to the lease and to case law, so put the answer in the lease (`eminent-domain-mi`).

The condemnation statutes protect a residential tenant in other ways. When the taking might require relocation, the condemning agency must tell the occupants in writing that an eminent domain proceeding has begun and what their basic rights are. An occupant who vacates is reimbursed by the public agency for reasonable and necessary moving expenses, up to $5,250 for an individual or family, or may take a fixed moving allowance, and an occupant of residential property with a leasehold interest of less than 6 months may instead elect a fixed payment of $3,500.

A residential occupant need not move until the moving payment is made and the occupant has had a reasonable opportunity, up to 180 days after it is paid, to relocate to a comparable replacement dwelling; where the agency follows federal relocation rules, those take precedence. The court in the condemnation case fixes the time and terms for surrendering possession.

A residential tenant's leasehold interest of less than 6 months is not a compensable claim in the condemnation case; for other interests, after the verdict the court, at any party's request, divides the award among the parties in interest, including a lessee, on the evidence they submit.

A lease term giving the lease's share of the award to you is common, but it is a tenant's waiver of a right the law provides, which Michigan's Consumer Protection Act allows only if it is clearly stated and the tenant specifically consents, so the library's clause leaves each of you to claim your own interest and never reaches the tenant's moving payments.

title: Agreed Notice Methods in Michigan
bodyText:
Michigan's landlord-tenant statutes do not use an "actual notice" standard, and no statute lets you and the tenant add a notice method, such as text message, across the board.

Whether you may agree on another method depends on the notice. A demand for possession or payment may be served only by personal delivery, by delivery at the premises to a household member or employee of suitable age and discretion with a request to pass it on, by first-class mail, or electronically if the tenant has specifically consented in writing through the exchange the statute describes; you may not refuse to rent because a prospective tenant declines electronic service (`electronic-service-consent-mi`). Notices the deposit law requires to be mailed, such as your itemized notice of damages, must still be mailed.

For notices no statute assigns a method, the lease may set the method, and Michigan's electronic transactions law lets an electronic record satisfy a writing requirement between parties who have agreed to deal electronically, provided the recipient can keep and print it. Two limits apply: a law that requires a particular sending method still controls, and a tenant who agreed to deal electronically may refuse further electronic transactions, a right the lease cannot waive.

The library's optional clause adds e-mail for lease notices that no law assigns a method (`agreed-notice-methods-mi`); give every eviction notice by a method the statute names and keep proof of service.

title: Online Tenant Portals in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute bars you from offering an online portal for rent, maintenance requests, signatures or notices, and none regulates portal fees as such. Three Michigan rules set the limits.

(1) Payment: if the lease allows more than one way to pay rent, at least one must carry no added charge or fee, and a lease term charging a fee on every allowed method is void, so a portal that charges a fee can be offered only alongside at least one way to pay that carries no fee, and a portal that charges a fee can never be the only way to pay (`acceptable-payment-methods-mi`).

(2) Electronic dealings: Michigan's electronic transactions law applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may refuse to deal electronically in later transactions; the lease cannot waive that right, so a term requiring every signature or notice to go through the portal cannot bind a tenant who later refuses.

(3) Statutory notices: a demand for possession may be served electronically only with the tenant's specific written consent given through the exchange the statute describes, and you may not refuse to rent because a prospective tenant declines (`electronic-service-consent-mi`); notices the deposit law requires to be mailed must still be mailed.

The deposit law does let you send the balance of a security deposit by direct deposit or electronic transfer to the tenant's bank account or an internet or mobile payment account or app, within 10 days after mailing the notice of damages, instead of enclosing a check (`security-deposit-return-mi`).

The library's optional clause keeps portal use voluntary (`tenant-portal-mi`).

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute bars lease terms that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or the reverse, and none limits how much more rent you may charge for one kind of lease than another (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched); local governments may not control the amount of rent (`edu-rent-control-mi`). The lease type still changes the rules that apply. A fixed term ends on its last day, while a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends on 1 month's notice, or notice equal to the rent interval where rent is paid at intervals of less than 3 months (`edu-tenancy-at-will-mi`). Whatever the type, a lease may not let you change its terms after the tenancy starts without the tenant's written consent, except the three 30-day adjustments (`edu-term-change-notice-mi`). Some options are open only to longer leases: you and the tenant may modify your repair covenants only where the lease has a current term of at least 1 year (`edu-habitability-modifiable-mi`), and the library offers its landlord casualty-termination clause only for terms of at least 1 year (`edu-casualty-short-term-mi`). Different terms may never rest on a protected trait, and if you hold 5 or more units, not on an applicant's lawful source of income (`edu-fair-housing-mi`, `edu-source-of-income-mi`).

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute sets a minimum type size or font for a whole residential lease, and none makes a lease, or a term in it, unenforceable or inadmissible because the print is small (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan's type rules reach particular notices instead. (1) The Truth in Renting Act notice must appear in a prominent place in the lease in type not smaller than 12-point, or in legible print with letters not smaller than 1/8 inch (`truth-in-renting-notice-mi`). (2) Your security deposit notice must include the forwarding-address statement in 12-point boldface type at least 4 points larger than the body of the notice or lease (`security-deposit-notice-mi`). (3) The move-in inventory checklist must carry its notice in 12-point boldface type at the top of the first page (`edu-condition-inspection-mi`). (4) Your notice of damages after move-out must include the response statement in 12-point boldface type at least 4 points larger than the body of the notice (`security-deposit-return-mi`). Michigan has no plain-language rule for leases (`edu-no-plain-language-rule-mi`). Readable type throughout is still the cautious course: a term buried in fine print invites a claim under the Consumer Protection Act (`edu-consumer-protection-mi`).

title: No Emergency Contact Statute in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires a lease to give an emergency or after-hours contact, a management website or a social-services hotline notice, and none requires you to post emergency contacts in the building.

Two rules make a working contact wise. Every lease must state the name and address at which the tenant gives you notices under the Truth in Renting Act (`lessor-notice-address-mi`), and your security deposit notice must give your name and address for communications (`security-deposit-notice-mi`). And you must keep the premises and common areas fit and in reasonable repair, which you cannot do for an urgent leak or no-heat call that no one answers.

So give tenants a number that is answered at all hours for emergencies.

A tenant's own emergency contact is a lease matter: the library's optional clause collects one for use only in an emergency (`emergency-contact-co`), and separately Michigan law gives the tenant the option to name a person you may contact if the tenant dies (`tenant-death-contact-mi`). Local housing codes may add posting rules; the library does not cover them.

title: No Renter's Insurance Statute in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute regulates renter's insurance in a residential lease. You may require it (`tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`), and nothing sets who chooses the insurer, a deadline for proof, force-placed or landlord-bought coverage, an administrative fee, or a required notice that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings. Michigan's general rules still apply.

(1) Put any insurance requirement, and its minimum coverage, in the lease when it is signed: during the term you may not add or change a lease term without the tenant's written consent, except the three 30-day adjustments, and the insurance-premium adjustment among them covers increases in your own liability, fire or worker compensation premiums, not a new tenant obligation.

(2) The library offers no clause letting you buy coverage when the tenant fails to and charge it back. Any such charge would have to be stated in the lease at signing and limited to the documented actual premium, and a person may not sell, solicit or negotiate insurance in Michigan without an insurance producer license; how that licensing rule treats a landlord who places coverage for a tenant is a question the library has not researched. Enforce the requirement as a lease term instead (`default-by-tenant-mi`).

(3) Do not tell the tenant that you are not liable for the tenant's property: a Michigan lease may not excuse you from liability for failing to perform, or negligently performing, a legal duty. Saying that your own insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings is a statement of fact, which the library's clause makes.

(4) If you have 5 or more units, apply the requirement the same way whatever an applicant's lawful source of income.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan does not require a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to tell tenants what insurance you carry, or to buy a policy with a relocation benefit for displaced tenants (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Statewide rental registration does not exist (`edu-landlord-registration-mi`); whether a city's registration or licensing ordinance asks for insurance is a local question the library has not researched. Your insurance still matters to the lease in two ways. During the term you may pass on increases in your liability, fire or worker compensation premiums only if the lease provides for it, on at least 30 days' written notice, and only to cover the added cost (`rent-cost-adjustment-mi`). And a Michigan lease may not excuse you from liability for your own failure to perform a legal duty; the one exception is a release for loss from fire or other casualty that the other party insures, under a policy that permits the waiver and waives the insurer's subrogation rights, and only to the extent of the insured party's recovery (`edu-exculpation-mi`, `edu-tenant-insurance-claims-mi`).

title: Tenant Insurance Claims and Fire Liability in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute says whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's own insurance, or how a claim affects the tenancy, and Michigan has no statute barring a landlord or its insurer from suing a tenant for an accidental fire (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Three rules shape what you can do. (1) Fire damage: a Michigan court has held that, absent an express and unequivocal agreement by the tenant to be liable, a tenant is not liable to the landlord or the landlord's fire insurer in negligence for fire damage the tenant caused; a lease term making the tenant liable for damage caused by the tenant's acts or omissions has been enforced as a contract. The library's optional clause makes the tenant liable for damage from deliberate, negligent or irresponsible conduct, other than ordinary wear and tear (`tenant-caused-damage-mi`, `edu-tenant-caused-damage-mi`). (2) Mutual release: the one exception to Michigan's ban on exculpatory lease terms lets a lease release a party from liability for loss from fire or other casualty that the other party insures, under a policy that permits the waiver and waives the insurer's subrogation rights, and only to the extent of the insured party's recovery. The library does not offer that release as a clause: for the tenant it waives a right the law provides, which Michigan's Consumer Protection Act allows only if clearly stated and specifically consented to, and it would narrow `tenant-caused-damage-mi`. A landlord who wants it should write it with advice (`edu-exculpation-mi`). (3) Your repair duties are yours: do not make repairs you owe depend on the tenant's insurance claim, since a lease may not alter the tenant's remedies when the premises are unfit (`edu-habitability-mi`). Any charge for your deductible or loss must be actual damages under the tenant-caused damage terms, not a fixed sum (`edu-liquidated-damages-mi`).

title: Disasters and Residential Leases in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute says what a declared disaster does to a residential lease: nothing ends the tenancy, stops rent while the home cannot be reached, sets debris or clean-up duties, or pauses evictions (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The ordinary rules decide it. If the building is destroyed or so damaged by the elements or any other cause that it is untenantable or unfit for occupancy, and the tenant was not at fault, the tenant may quit and surrender possession and owes no rent after surrender, unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing (`edu-casualty-mi`). You must keep the premises and common areas fit for their intended use and in reasonable repair, and a lease may not alter the tenant's remedies when they are not (`edu-habitability-mi`); for a lease of at least 1 year the library's optional clause lets you end the lease if the home cannot reasonably be repaired within the period you set (`casualty-termination-mi`). Where the Housing Law applies, rent rules for premises an enforcing agency finds unfit also apply (`edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-mi`). You may not lock a tenant out or remove belongings without a court order (`edu-self-help-eviction-mi`). One disaster rule binds everyone: during a declared state of disaster or emergency the Governor may control the occupancy of premises in a stricken or threatened area, order evacuations and provide temporary emergency housing, and willfully disobeying such an order is a misdemeanor, so follow any order that reaches your property. Charging a price grossly in excess of what similar property rents for can violate the Consumer Protection Act (`edu-consumer-protection-mi`).

title: No Disaster Guest Rule in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, limits how long such guests may stay, or says that a displaced person staying in someone's home does not become a tenant (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The Governor's emergency powers include providing temporary emergency housing, but they do not direct private landlords to accept guests. Your lease terms apply as written: guests and occupants are governed by your guest and occupancy terms (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`, `permitted-occupants`, `edu-no-guest-rights-statute-mi`). Michigan's crime of occupying a single-family or 2-family dwelling without the owner's consent does not apply to a guest or family member of a tenant, so removing an overstaying displaced guest runs through the lease and, if needed, the courts (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-mi`). Apply your rules the same way to everyone, without regard to a protected trait such as familial status (`edu-fair-housing-mi`). If a tenant asks to take in displaced family or friends, the practical course is a short written permission that names them and sets an end date, so they stay guests rather than becoming occupants or tenants; Michigan's relocation assistance law reaches people displaced by public acquisition and by code enforcement or a governmental rehabilitation program, not by a disaster as such.

title: No Tenant Purchase Right in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan gives tenants no right to buy, or to receive an offer on, a rental property you plan to sell, and no right of first refusal; there is no District of Columbia-style tenant opportunity to purchase law (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan also has no statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law for ordinary tenancies, and local governments may not control rents, so no lease notice about rent limits, just cause or a purchase right is required (`edu-no-good-cause-notice-mi`, `edu-rent-control-mi`). Three nearby rules are narrower. (1) Since July 21, 2026, a large institutional investor (one with investment control of more than 100 single-family homes in Michigan and $375 million or more under management or in net value) may not buy a single-family home, meaning a structure with 2 or fewer dwelling units and not a manufactured home, unless an exception applies; one exception is a purchase under a homeownership program that, among other things, gives renters a right of first refusal and a 30-day first look. That is a condition of the investor's exception, not a right Michigan gives tenants generally (`edu-single-family-rental-limits-mi`). (2) Urban homestead programs in public housing let qualified residents rent and then buy, and give the resident organization a 5-year right of first refusal on resale. (3) In a condominium conversion the developer must give tenants notice and time to stay, not a right to buy (`edu-condo-conversion-mi`). If you give a tenant an option to purchase a 1-to-4-unit home, the seller disclosure rules apply (`edu-optional-lease-terms-mi`). When you sell, the lease and deposit obligations pass as described in `edu-deposit-on-sale-mi`.

title: No Exemption Notice Needed in Michigan
bodyText: Because Michigan has no statewide rent cap, no just-cause eviction law for ordinary houses and apartments and no tenant right to buy, there is nothing for a property to be exempt from, and no lease or notice statement of exemption is required (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Local governments may not enact or enforce rules controlling the amount of rent for private residential property (`edu-rent-control-mi`), and the library's Michigan rows on just cause and purchase rights say the same (`edu-no-good-cause-notice-mi`, `edu-no-tenant-purchase-right-mi`). Leave other states' exemption notices out of a Michigan lease: a statement about a law Michigan does not have only confuses the tenant. Two Michigan tenancies are different, because the eviction statute requires just cause to end them: tenancies in housing operated by a city, village, township, county or housing commission, and mobile home park tenancies (`edu-for-cause-eviction-mi`). Neither carries an exemption statement.

title: No Sunset of Michigan Tenant Laws
