bodyText: As of November 13, 2026, none of Michigan's core landlord-tenant statutes is scheduled to expire: the Truth in Renting Act, the security deposit law, the repair covenants, the notice-to-quit statute, the summary proceedings chapter, the lockout statute, the civil rights acts' housing provisions and the ban on local rent control carry no repeal date (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan has no tenant protection act like California's to expire. Recent changes are permanent and already in effect: since September 21, 2026, a lease may not put an added fee on every way it allows rent to be paid, so at least one allowed way must be free of any added charge or fee, even if it is the only one (`acceptable-payment-methods-mi`), and the deposit return rules allow electronic refunds (`security-deposit-return-mi`). The Legislature can amend these laws in any session, and the library rechecks them on each review.

title: Out-of-State Owners in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan does not make an owner who lives outside Michigan appoint a Michigan agent, name one in the lease, or file anything before renting or suing, and it does not make your tenant withhold income tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). What every owner must do, wherever you live: state in the lease the name and address at which the tenant gives you notices under the Truth in Renting Act (`lessor-notice-address-mi`), and, if you hold a security deposit, give the tenant the written deposit notice with your name and address for communications within 14 days after the tenant takes possession (`security-deposit-notice-mi`). Where the Housing Law applies and the local enforcing agency keeps an owner registry, the owner of a multiple dwelling or rooming house must register the address of the owner's residence or usual place of business and the name of any managing agent; anyone who manages for you for a fee needs a real estate licence (`edu-landlord-registration-mi`). Being sued here: owning, using or possessing real property in Michigan, or transacting business here, lets a Michigan court exercise personal jurisdiction over you for claims arising from it. Court papers may be served on an individual owner, resident or not, by personal delivery or by registered or certified mail restricted to you; on a nonresident individual also by serving your agent, employee or representative in Michigan and mailing a copy by registered mail to your last known address; on an agent you have appointed in writing to receive service; and, if those cannot reasonably be done, in another manner the court orders. Entity owners: a corporation or limited liability company is served through an officer, manager or its resident agent, and an out-of-state corporation, limited liability company or limited partnership that transacts business in Michigan without registering may not sue here until it registers, and a business name must be filed before suing on contracts made under it (`edu-entity-landlord-court-representation-mi`). Reporting duties that bind every person, such as reporting certain deaths to the medical examiner, bind you and your staff (`edu-law-enforcement-cooperation-mi`). A lease may name your local manager for notices, but it may not appoint anyone to accept court papers for the tenant (`edu-eviction-service-party-mi`).

title: Checked Outside the Landlord-Tenant Statutes
bodyText: These questions were checked across the whole Michigan Compiled Laws and Constitution, not only the landlord-tenant statutes. (1) Squatters: present, through the courts and the criminal law, not a police fast track. A person who occupies a single-family home or a unit of a 2-family home without ever having occupied it with the owner's consent for an agreed price commits a crime (a misdemeanor for a first offense, a felony after that), but the crime does not reach a guest or family member of the owner or of a tenant. You may recover possession from someone who took it by forcible entry or by trespass without color of title by summary proceedings, and the court may issue the writ immediately after the judgment if that is pleaded and proved (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-mi`). No Michigan statute lets the police remove an occupant on your sworn statement without a court order. Tenants and former tenants are removed only by eviction (`edu-eviction-process-mi`). (2) Cash receipts: no Michigan statute requires you to give a receipt for rent, in cash or otherwise, and no general statute makes every creditor give one (`edu-no-rent-receipt-rule-mi`); give one anyway, since in a nonpayment case the proof is yours to produce. (3) Registration before eviction: no Michigan statute makes landlord registration, a rental licence or a certificate of compliance a condition of filing for or getting a judgment for possession; the Housing Law certificate cuts the other way, since a court may issue a writ immediately where the premises lack a required certificate and have been ordered vacated. City registration ordinances are local law the library has not researched (`edu-landlord-registration-mi`). Business filings can still stop a suit: an unregistered out-of-state entity, or a business name that was not filed, may not sue until it complies (`edu-entity-landlord-court-representation-mi`). (4) Suing or serving someone outside Michigan: owning or using real property here, or doing business here, lets a Michigan court hear claims arising from it, and court papers may be served on a nonresident by the methods the court rules allow (`edu-nonresident-owner-agent-mi`). (5) Reporting duties that bind every person, such as reporting certain deaths, are in `edu-law-enforcement-cooperation-mi`.

title: Construction Liens for Tenant Work in Michigan
bodyText:
Michigan's Construction Lien Act gives a contractor, subcontractor, supplier or laborer who provides an improvement to real property a lien on the interest of the owner or lessee who contracted for it, on the interest of an owner who subordinated its interest to the mortgage for the improvement, and on the interest of an owner who required the improvement.

When your tenant hires the work, the lien attaches to the tenant's interest (the leasehold), including any interest the tenant later acquires, not to your ownership. Your ownership is exposed if you required the improvement, so do not make the lease require the tenant to improve the property unless you accept that risk; whether consenting to an alteration, or a lease term permitting one, counts as requiring it is case law.

Ending the lease does not defeat the lien on the improvement itself, and a lien claimant who gave the required notice and performs the lease covenants within 30 days after actual notice of the termination steps into the tenant's rights under the lease as they stood just before it ended. Where property is leased by more than one person, a co-tenant is presumed to have consented to work another co-tenant contracted for.

A contractor has no lien on a residential structure (a condominium unit or a building with no more than 2 units, in which the contracting owner or lessee lives or will live) unless the work was done under a written contract carrying the licensing statement the Act requires.

Michigan has no notice of nonresponsibility that lets an owner who did not contract for the work protect its interest, and a contract for an improvement may not require a lien waiver before the work is done, so a lease cannot take away a contractor's lien rights; it can only set the duties between you and the tenant. The library's optional clause does that (`no-liens-mi`), and approved alterations are governed by `no-alterations`.

title: No Animal-Care Entry Right in Michigan
bodyText:
Michigan gives you no special right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal when the tenant is hospitalized, detained or otherwise away, and no procedure for taking custody of it.

Your ordinary entry rules apply: where the Housing Law applies you must request and obtain the tenant's permission before entering except in an emergency, and the library's Michigan entry clause asks permission on 24 hours' notice everywhere (`landlords-access-mi`). Whether a lease term can give that permission in advance is not settled by the statute; trying to reach the tenant first is the cautious course, and an animal left without care may also be a matter for animal control or the police.

The library's optional animal-care clause (`animal-care-access-vi`) has the tenant name a person to care for or remove the animals and consent to your letting that person in, and if no one can be reached lets you ask animal control, a peace officer or an animal shelter to take charge.

Michigan's animal law is why the named person or animal control should act rather than you: an owner, possessor or person having the charge or custody of an animal must give it adequate care (food, water, shelter, sanitary conditions, exercise and veterinary attention) and may not abandon it without providing for its care, and under the Dog Law a person who keeps or harbors a dog or has it in their care is its owner for licensing and liability. Michigan's animal control officers and its animal control and animal protection shelters are the local authorities.

Your pet clause already says you will not seize or remove a pet without a court order and does not limit animal control acting on its own authority (`pet-policy-mi`). This does not apply to a service or assistance animal, which follows `assistance-animal-accommodation`.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan does not require you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or notice about pets and eviction, with the lease or at any other time, even when you know the tenant has a dog or cat (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan also has no special rule for animals on the day an eviction order is carried out. The order directs the court officer, bailiff, sheriff or police officer to remove all occupants and all personal property, leaving the property in an area open to the public or the public right-of-way or delivering it to the sheriff, and the officer decides whether the premises and property are abandoned (`edu-post-eviction-property-mi`); the statute does not say how a live animal is handled. Because a person in charge of an animal must give it adequate care and may not abandon it without providing for its care, the cautious course is to ask the officer, before the eviction is carried out, to arrange for animal control to take any animal left behind, and never to take custody yourself (`edu-no-animal-care-entry-right-mi`, `pet-policy-mi`). Telling a tenant in a nonpayment or other eviction case to make arrangements for pets is good practice, not a statutory duty.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute says whether a tenant who rents a home with farmland or acreage gets the right to hunt, fish or trap there, or whether that right stays with you unless you grant it in writing, so the lease decides.

Michigan's recreational trespass law matters here. No one may enter farm property, or property that is fenced to keep out intruders or posted against entry, for hunting, fishing, trapping or other recreation without the consent of the owner or the owner's lessee or agent. So a tenant in possession can give that consent unless the lease says otherwise. Consent may be oral or written and may set conditions, and if the owner or lessee requires written consent from everyone, a person on the land without it is presumed to be there unlawfully. Only the owner, or the owner's lessee or agent, may post or fence another's land against hunting.

A separate safety rule protects your tenant's home: no one may hunt with a firearm within 150 yards of an occupied dwelling, or a barn or other farm building, without the written permission of the owner, renter or occupant, so if you or your guests hunt near the house, get the tenant's written permission.

An owner, tenant or lessee is not liable to someone using the land for hunting or other outdoor recreation without paying for it, except for gross negligence or willful and wanton misconduct.

If you want to keep the hunting, fishing and trapping rights, say so in the lease (`farmland-sporting-rights-mi`).

title: Housing Your Own Employee in Michigan
bodyText: Michigan has no statute on housing you provide to your own employee, such as a resident manager, caretaker or farm worker. Nothing requires a signed disclosure of the conditions for occupying and vacating the unit, nothing requires you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, and the eviction statute has no employee exception (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Summary proceedings reach any person who holds over after the lease ends, after a power to terminate in the lease, or after a notice to quit, so treat an employee who lives in your unit as a tenant: put the arrangement in a written rental agreement that states the rent, or that the housing is part of the pay, and how and when occupancy ends with the job; end it by the lease's terms or a proper notice and, if needed, through the court, never by a lockout (`edu-landlord-remedies-termination-mi`, `edu-self-help-eviction-mi`). If rent is to come out of wages, Michigan's wage law forbids deductions without the employee's full, free and written consent obtained without intimidation; a deduction for your benefit needs written consent for each wage payment it applies to and may not bring pay below the state minimum wage. Housing for 5 or more migratory agricultural workers is an agricultural labor camp, which may be operated only under a state license posted at the camp, with 30 days' written notice to the department before building, enlarging or converting one. Local ordinances may add rules; the library does not cover them.

title: Informal Dispute Resolution Terms in Michigan
bodyText:
No Michigan statute requires, permits or limits a lease term asking you and your tenant to try to settle a dispute informally before going to court, so such a term is an ordinary contract term, with the Truth in Renting Act's limits. A Michigan lease may not waive or alter a party's right to a jury or any other right of notice or procedure required by law in a court case under the lease, may not waive or alter rights in eviction (summary) proceedings, and may not alter the tenant's remedies when the premises are unfit; a term that does is void and exposes you to the Act's remedies.

So keep an informal step non-binding and keep possession and emergencies out of it. The library's optional clause does this: either party gives written notice of a dispute and offers to meet within 10 days, but failing to do so is no defense and delays nothing (`informal-dispute-resolution-mi`).

The Act has its own pre-suit step that the lease cannot change: before suing over an unlawful lease term, the tenant generally gives you written notice and 20 days to cure it. Michigan's community dispute resolution program funds local centers that offer voluntary mediation and conciliation as an alternative to court.

Binding arbitration is a different thing, and the library does not offer it for Michigan.

title: Usufruct and Life Estates in Michigan
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Michigan property law does not use; the word appears nowhere in the Michigan Compiled Laws or Constitution, so civil-law rules about leases granted by a usufructuary do not apply here (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The closest Michigan interest is a life estate, for example a parent who deeded a house to the children but kept the right to live in it for life. A life tenant who rents the property out is a landlord with all the ordinary duties, because Michigan's deposit law treats the owner, lessor or sublessor, or anyone managing the unit, as the landlord. One statute speaks to the lease itself: a conveyance by a tenant for life that purports to grant a greater estate than the life tenant has does not forfeit the life estate but passes only what the life tenant could lawfully convey. In that statute a conveyance does not include a lease for a term of 3 years or less, so it reaches only longer leases. No Michigan statute says what happens to a shorter lease when the life estate ends, whether the lease binds the people who then own the property, or what the life tenant must tell the tenant; that is case law. The cautious course for a life tenant is to have the remainder owners sign the lease, or to tell the tenant in writing that the lease may end when the life estate ends. A life tenant who commits or allows waste is liable for double the actual damages.

title: No Special District Lease Statement in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a residential lease to state that a rental sits in a special assessment district, a downtown development authority, a business improvement district or another special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges or rules, and none gives a tenant a role in district decisions because of the tenancy (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). The one lease rule found is commercial: in a principal shopping district designated after July 14, 1992, a lessor may revise an existing lease to a business on the parcel to recover all or part of the special assessment. It does not reach leases of homes. For a residential lease, keep district charges in the rent you set at signing. During the term, the Truth in Renting Act lets a lease pass on increases in ad valorem property taxes, listed utility charges and listed insurance premiums on 30 days' written notice (`rent-cost-adjustment-mi`); a special assessment is levied on the basis of the special benefit to the parcel, not its value, so whether it counts as an ad valorem tax increase is doubtful, and the cautious course is not to pass it on mid-term (`edu-term-change-notice-mi`).

title: No Communal Land Lease Approval in Michigan
bodyText: No Michigan statute requires a government officer to approve a lease of communal, tribal or Indian-owned land before it is valid, and none says what happens to rent or possession before approval (Michigan Compiled Laws, Constitution and 2025-2026 acts searched). Michigan has no communal land system of its own. Land held in trust by the United States for a tribe or an individual Indian, or subject to a federal restriction on transfer, is governed by federal and tribal law: federal law generally requires the approval of the Secretary of the Interior for a lease of restricted Indian land, but a tribe may lease its own land for residential purposes without that approval under tribal leasing regulations the Secretary has approved (individually owned allotted land excepted), and the federal regulations and tribal law were not read. Michigan's Indian housing authority law lets an authority lease and operate housing projects, but it sets no approval rule for private leases. If you rent property that may be trust or restricted land, check with the tribe and the Bureau of Indian Affairs before signing.

title: Confirmed Absences, Miscellaneous
bodyText: These are questions in this group that Michigan law does not answer, each checked across the whole Michigan Compiled Laws, the 1963 Constitution and the 2025-2026 acts as held, not only the landlord-tenant statutes. Where a row is named, it gives the detail and what Michigan does have nearby. (1) Lease form: no statute regulates automatic-renewal clauses, sets a minimum type size for the whole lease, or requires parity between month-to-month and fixed-term terms (`edu-no-automatic-renewal-rule-mi`, `edu-no-lease-type-size-rule-mi`, `edu-no-lease-type-parity-rule-mi`). (2) Guarantors: no lease-guaranty statute; only the writing rule and the cosigner notice law apply (`edu-guarantor-renewal-mi`). (3) Notices: no actual-notice standard or general agreed-method rule, no portal statute, no emergency-contact rule (`edu-actual-notice-method-mi`, `edu-tenant-portal-mi`, `edu-no-emergency-contact-rule-mi`). (4) Proceedings: no landlord duty to disclose foreclosure and no landlord or tenant duty to give notice of other proceedings (`edu-no-foreclosure-disclosure-mi`, `edu-adverse-proceeding-notice-mi`); no statute on what a taking does to a lease or its rent (`edu-eminent-domain-mi`). (5) Insurance: no renter's-insurance statute, no landlord insurance mandate and no accidental-fire statute (`edu-no-renters-insurance-rule-mi`, `edu-no-landlord-liability-insurance-mi`, `edu-tenant-insurance-claims-mi`). (6) Disasters: no rule ending a tenancy or stopping rent because of a declared disaster, and none on housing displaced guests (`edu-disaster-duties-mi`, `edu-no-disaster-guest-rule-mi`). (7) Purchase rights: no tenant right to buy, no exemption notice and no sunset of core tenant laws (`edu-no-tenant-purchase-right-mi`, `edu-no-tpa-exemption-notice-mi`, `edu-no-tenant-law-sunset-mi`). (8) Out-of-state owners: no in-state agent, filing or rent-withholding rule (`edu-nonresident-owner-agent-mi`); no registration precondition to an eviction (`edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-mi`). (9) Construction liens: no notice of nonresponsibility (`edu-construction-liens-mi`). (10) Animals: no landlord entry or custody right for a tenant's animal and no pet or eviction fact sheet (`edu-no-animal-care-entry-right-mi`, `edu-no-pet-eviction-fact-sheet-mi`). (11) Rural land: no default allocation of hunting, fishing or trapping rights (`edu-farmland-hunting-rights-mi`). (12) Employee housing: no occupancy disclosure, offer or caretaker eviction rule (`edu-tenant-employee-housing-mi`). (13) Pre-suit resolution: no statute on informal-resolution lease terms (`edu-informal-dispute-resolution-mi`). (14) Usufruct and life estates: no usufruct, and no statute on a shorter lease granted by a life tenant when the life estate ends (`edu-no-usufructuary-lessor-mi`). (15) Special districts: no residential lease statement or tenant role (`edu-no-special-district-statement-mi`). (16) Tribal land: no state approval rule; federal and tribal law, not read, may apply (`edu-no-communal-land-lease-approval-mi`). An absence here means no statute; case law, administrative rules other than those held, court rules other than those read and local ordinances were not read, and where one of them could matter the named row says so.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Michigan follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 440.3311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Mich. Comp. Laws § 440.1308(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Michigan's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Truth in Renting Act, the landlord-tenant relationships act and the summary proceedings chapter searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Michigan's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
